Leave granted.
We have heard the learned senior counsel and
learned counsel appearing for the appellants and the
respondents.
By the impugned judgment(s), the High Court was

## Page 85

3
pleased to restore the Award of the Land Acquisition
Collector, which had fixed the Award at Rs.30 lakhs
per acre.
The date of the Notification under Section 4 of
the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 (hereinafter referred
to as  ‘the Act,  1894’) is  24.05.2011. The  Land
Acquisition Collector had taken into consideration
the  date  of  the  sale  deed  produced  by  the
respondents, while ignoring the documents produced by
the appellants. However, the Reference Court vide
order  dated  03.07.2017  took  into  consideration
Exhibit P-4/C, which was the sale deed produced by
the appellants pertaining to the same village that
has been subjected to acquisition. While doing so,
the Reference Court, after having found that the
aforesaid sale deed, relied upon by the appellants,
was for a smaller extent of land being nearer to the
main road, and applied 50% deduction as development
charges.
Suffice it is to state that the Reference Court
had consciously not considered the enhancement, as
the sale deed relied upon by the appellants was of
the year 2010, while acquisition was of the year
2011, though the difference is only 6 months. 
Learned  senior  counsel  appearing  for  the
appellants would submit that, apart from the view of
the Reference Court having accepted the sale deed of

## Page 86

4
the highest value, the fact remains that there is no
dispute with respect to the land, which was subject
matter of the sale deed (Exhibit P-4/C), relied upon
by the appellants, being situated within the same
village which has been subjected to acquisition.
Therefore, an amount higher than the Award fixed by
the  Land  Acquisition  Collector  will  have  to  be
granted by setting aside the order of the High Court,
particularly, when there is an error in relying upon
the sale deed produced post the date of Notification
and for a lesser value.  
Learned counsel appearing for the respondents
would submit that there is no bar in relying upon the
sale deed post the date of notification. The High
Court was right in holding that the location of the
lands in the sale deed relied upon by the appellants
has not been proved by them, and in such view of the
matter, there is no need for interference with the
impugned judgment.
For deciding the just and fair compensation, the
Court  will  have  to  sit  in  the  armchair  of  the
intending seller and the purchaser. For doing so, the
land which is getting the highest valuation must be
taken into consideration. Thereafter, the relevant
factors such as the proximity, the nature of the land
along with its character ought to be seen.  The date
of the sale deed relied upon is also a relevant

## Page 87

5
factor. In our considered view, the Reference Court
correctly  took  into  consideration  the  relevant
materials.  As  rightly  submitted  by  the  learned
counsel appearing for the appellants, there is no
dispute with respect to the admitted fact that the
sale deed relied upon by the appellants i.e. Exhibit
P-4/C, pertains to the land situated in the very same
village. The Reference Court has rightly deducted 50%
as  development  charges.  Even  assuming  that  the
potential value of the said land is higher, an extent
of land is required for fixing the valuation. This
has rightly been done by the Reference Court.
Though further enhancement has been sought for
by the appellants based upon the year of the sale
deed relied upon vis-a-vis the date of Notification,
the difference being six months, we are not inclined
to accept the said contention.
In such view of the matter, we set aside the
impugned judgment(s) of the High Court and restore
the order dated 03.07.2017 and order dated 08.12.2017
of the Reference Court awarding Rs.54 lakhs per acre.
The  appeals  stand  allowed  in  part,  in  the
aforesaid terms.
No order as to costs.
Pending  application(s),  if  any,  shall  stand
disposed of.

the deduction of 50% has admittedly been made from
the market value indicated by the circle rate. If
that is taken into consideration, the Award passed by
the  Reference  Court  is  perfectly  in  order  and,
therefore, the same can be taken as just and fair
compensation.

the Reference Court and the consequent Award passed.

The lands in these appeals have been acquired

maintenance,  management  and  operation  of  a  road

post Notification dated sale deed, registered after a
month. The High Court, in turn, was pleased to rely
upon the post Notification dated sale deed produced
by the Requisitioning body, and accordingly restored
the  valuation  fixed  by  the  Land  Acquisition
Collector. 
In our considered view, both the High Court and
the Reference Court committed an error. The highest
value of the land available before the Court will
have to be considered. Added to that, we find that
even as admitted by the witnesses who spoke on behalf

10
of the respondents, the market value was much higher
than the valuation fixed by the Land Acquisition
Collector.

the  Reference  Court  into  consideration,  we  are
inclined to do a guess work, as that valuation is
obviously  the  commercial  rate  and,  therefore,  a
certain deduction is required to be made. However,
the valuation fixed at Rs.40 lakhs per acre can never
be accepted at all.
In  such  view  of  the  matter,  the  impugned
judgment(s) passed by the High Court stand set aside.
Accordingly, we deem it just and proper to fix the
compensation at Rs.75 lakhs per acre.

terms.

entitled to all the consequential statutory benefits.

disposed of.

relied upon, being much anterior to the date on which
the land was acquired, only a 10% deduction has been
made.  The  Reference  Court  rightly  took  into
consideration the one and a half year gap between the
date of the Notification and the date of the Sale
deed.

1) Leave granted.
2) The present appeal calls in question the correctness of the
judgment dated 20.03.2024 in Writ Appeal No.2420 of 2023 passed
by the High Court of Judicature at Madras.  By the said judgment, the
Division Bench set aside the order of the learned Single Judge in Writ
Petition No.20394/2023 dated 11.07.2023.
3) The Writ Petition No.20394/2023 was filed to call in question,
the Order dated 25.04.2023 passed by the Sub-Registrar, Kotagiri
Taluk, Nilgiris, refusing to receive and register the settlement deed
dated 25.04.2023, executed by the writ petitioner in favour of Mrs. S.
Rani, settling an extent of 20.75 cents of the land. The learned Single
Judge concluded that the refusal check slip issued by the Sub-
1

## Page 147

Registrar, based on the objections of the Block Development Officer,
Kotagiri was justified. However, the learned Single Judge also held
that if there are any civil remedies to be adjudicated, the writ
petitioner was at liberty to pursue the same.
4) The Division Bench, while setting aside the Order of the learned
Single Judge, in paragraph 9 recorded as follows:
“9. When the competent Court of law have already adjudicated
the claim of the Block Development Officer and have also passed
a final decree proceedings in the partition suit, we are unable to
comprehend as to how there could exist any disputed fact at all.
As a matter of fact, the parties to the suit proceedings are bound
by the final decree proceedings and thus would be entitled to
deal with their respective shares over the subject properties in
accordance  with the terms of the decree.  When there are no
disputed facts and the claim of the Block Development Officer
over the subject lands have also been finally adjudicated and
rejected, there was no authority or legal claim for the Block
Development Officer to raise any objection with the Registering
Authority to stall registration of any sort  of  document  over  the
partition  suit properties. Consequently, the refusal check slip,
which  was  impugned  in  the  Writ  Petition,  cannot  be  legally
sustained.”
5) A close reading of paragraph 9 of the impugned order reveals that
the Division Bench proceeded on the basis that a competent Court of law
has already adjudicated the claim of the Block Development Officer and
passed a final decree proceeding in the partition suit. In view of the same,
the Division Bench held that it was difficult to comprehend as to how
there could exist any dispute at all.
2

## Page 148

6) The Division Bench further held that the parties to the suit are bound
by the final decree proceedings and would be entitled to deal with their
respective shares over the subject properties.
7) The Division Bench further held that there were no disputed
questions of fact involved and the claim of the Block Development Officer
on the subject land being finally adjudicated and rejected, the Block
Development Officer had no authority or legal claim to raise any
objection.
8) Heard learned counsel for the parties.
9) When questions were put to the learned senior counsel for the
respondent(s) as to on what basis the Division Bench has held that the
Competent Court of law has concluded the issue in favour of the writ
petitioner, learned senior counsel drew our attention to the issues raised
and the findings in the judgment dated 16.09.1978 in Original Suit
No.182/1977 passed by the Subordinate Judge, Nilgiris, Ootacamund.
10) Learned Senior Counsel for the respondent(s) contended that the
appellant herein was defendant no.26 and that the findings of the Civil
Court has conclusively negated their claim to the suit property. For the
sake of convenience, we extract herein below, the issues 1, 2, 3, 7 and an
additional issue framed in O.S. No.182/1977 :-
3

## Page 149

“4.  The following issues have been framed for trial:-
1. Whether  the  gift  deed  dated  13.12.1976  has  not
conferred title or possession to any portion of the land
to the 26th defendant?
2. Whether the gift deed is invalid, in effective and in
operative?
3. Whether the 26th defendant is not entitled to the suit
property measuring 1.25 1/2 acres of land?
***
7. To what relief are the plaintiffs entitled?
Additional issue: -
   1. Whether the suit as framed is not maintainable against
the defendants 6 to 26?”
11) Further, in paragraph 5 of the judgment in Original Suit
No.182/1977, the aforesaid issues came to be discussed in the
following terms:
"5.  Issues 1 to 3 and Additional issue :  It may at the outset be
stated that the issues 1 to 3 may not arise for consideration in as
much as, as rightly contended on behalf of the learned counsel for
the defendants 6 to 26, the  suit as framed  is not maintainable
against them. It should be remembered that it is the definite case
of the plaintiffs, that by virtue of a family arrangement in the
family of the parties about hundred years ago, the entire extent of
the suit property was allotted to the ancestor of the plaintiffs and
defendants 1 to 5 and it is only the plaintiffs and the defendants 1
to 5 that have been in joint possession and enjoyment of the
entirety of  the  suit  property,  and  that  the  defendants  6  to 25
have absolutely no right to any portion of the suit property and
that the gift deed alleged to have been executed by them in
respect of the moiety of the suit property in favour of the 26th
defendant is absolutely void. In short, their case is that the
defendants 6 to 26 have no interest whatsoever in the suit
property. Thus, on their own case, the defendants 6 to 26 are not
at all necessary parties to the suit for partition. It is well settled
that in a partition suit only the co-sharers are necessary parties
and not the persons who have absolutely no interest in the
common property. But the contention that has been advanced on
behalf of the plaintiffs is that even though the defendants 6 to 26
are not necessary parties for the relief of partition, they have been
impleaded for the purpose of getting a relief of injunction against
4

## Page 150

them since  they  have  been  interfering  with  their possession and
enjoyment of the suit property. I am afraid that this contention
cannot also be accepted in as much as it should be remembered
that  the  injunction  is  prayed  for  only  with  reference  to  the
plaintiffs.  In  other  words,  the  plaintiffs  have  prayed  that  the
defendants 6 to 26 should be injuncted from interfering with their
possession and enjoyment of the suit property. It is no doubt true
that one of the co-owners can sustain an action against a stranger
for injunction in respect of a common property. But even then, the
suit should be on behalf of the co-owners. But it is  significant  to
note  that  in  this  case,  the relief of injunction has been prayed
for only for the purpose of restraining the defendants 6 to 26 from
interfering with the possession of the plaintiffs and not that of the
defendants 1 to 5, who according to the plaintiffs, are also co-
sharers in respect of the suit property. That apart, the plaintiffs
claim  only  1/3rd  share  in  the  suit  property  and  unless  a  final
decree  is  passed,  it  cannot  be  said  which  portion  of  the  suit
property will be allotted to them and that being so now, the relief
for injunction is premature.  The only remedy that is open to the
plaintiffs is either to file a suit for declaration and for the
consequential relief of injunction along with the defendants 1 to
5 against the defendant 6 to 26 or to get a final decree for
partition of their 1/3 share in this suit and get the property
allotted to their share and thereafter, if need be, to file a suit
against the other defendants for the relief of injunction. As the
matters now stand, I am clearly of the opinion that the suit is not
sustainable and maintainable against the defendants 6 to 26. In
this view, I hold that issues 1 to 3 do not arise for consideration,
while the additional issue is answered in the affirmative."
12) It is based on this judgment that the parties claim final decree
proceedings have been drawn up.

15. On a perusal of the preliminary decree passed in O.S.No.182
of 1977, it is evident that the Panchayat Union Council, Kotagiri
represented by its Commissioner is the 26th defendant in the suit.
Therefore,  the  contention  of  the  petitioners  that  the  suit  for
partition  was  filed  even  without  impleading  them,  cannot  be
accepted. In fact, in the preliminary decree, as already stated, the
suit was dismissed as against the defendants 6 to 26. Though the
preliminary decree was passed in the year 1978, the final decree
was passed only on 15.07.2014 (i.e.) after 35 years.
16.It is also pertinent to note that the preliminary decree passed in
O.S.No.182 of 1977 was not challenged by the parties and the
same became final. Subsequent to the order passed in the C.R.P.
(NPD).No.4721 of 2012, final decree application in I.A.No.307 of
2012 was again taken on file by the trial Court and an Advocate
Commissioner was appointed for partitioning the suit property into
three equal shares as per the preliminary decree. Subsequently, the
Commissioner filed his report and a final decree was also passed.
The petitioners are now claiming 1.25 ½ acres out of the total
extent  of  2.51  acres.  Since  the  preliminary  decree  was  not
challenged by the petitioners, now they cannot seek for impleading
themselves in the final decree proceedings. The trial Court has to
pass the final decree only in terms of the preliminary decree and
the trial Court cannot deviate from the preliminary decree. If the
petitioners are having any right in respect of 1.25 ½ acres of land
out of the total extent of 2.51 acres, it is open to them to get their
rights  declared  in  an  appropriate  proceedings.  Since  the  trial
Court had already passed a final decree, the present application
filed by the revision petitioners to get themselves impleaded in the
final decree application cannot stand. The trial Court has rightly
dismissed the application.
30) It further appears that the said original defendants – Defendant
Nos. 6 to 25/ LRs of original defendants filed O.S. No. 207 of 2013
seeking the declaration of decree dated 16.09.1978 in O.S.No. 182 of
1977 as null and void and also prayed for a declaration that the gift
settlement deed in favour of the appellant as null and void and sought
partition of the suit property.  The prayer is extracted hereinbelow: -
23

## Page 169

“The  plaintiffs  therefore  pray  that  this  Hon'ble  Court  may  be
pleased to pass a decree and judgment. 
a. For a preliminary decree for partition dividing the suit schedule
properties  by  metes  and  bounds  and  allot  80  1/2  cents  to  the
plaintiffs as their shares. 
b. Appoint a court commissioner to effect just and proper division
and allot and deliver the plaintiffs' share.
c. For declaration that the preliminary decree and judgment passed
in  O.S.  No.  182/1977  dated  16-9-1978  on  the  file  of  the  Sub
Ordinate Court, Udhagamandalam as null and void. 
d. For declaration  that  the  gift  settlement  deed  dated  13-12-1976
registered as D. No. 814/1976 on the file of the Sub Registrar
Office, Kotagiri executed by the defendants 26 to 29 and others to
31st defendant as partily null and void upto the plaintiff’s shares. 
e. Grant such further and other relieves as the Hon'ble Court may be
deem fit to grant and finally adjudicate the matter in the interest of
justice.”
31)  It transpires from the record that this suit has now ultimately
been rejected under Order VII Rule 11 and the same was upheld by
the Appellate Court. There is no information as to whether the matter
was carried further and as to what was the fate, if so.  Be that as it
may, this aspect need not detain the Court.  
32) The historical narration of these facts is only for completion of
the factual aspect.  The fact remains that as far as the appellant is
concerned, there has been no adjudication on the validity of the gift
deed.  The gift deed has not been set aside.  Secondly, the plea set up
against the appellant by the respondents-settlor herein Ramakrishnan,
namely, the original  Defendant Nos. 1 to 5, including the LRs based
on the family arrangement between the family of Hutcha and Puria
24

## Page 170

Nanja has not been adjudicated.  Thirdly, the plea of adverse
possession set up by the plaintiff against the appellant and  Defendant
Nos. 6 to 25 has also been negated in the suit.  The suit was dismissed
against the appellant as well as against the original Defendant Nos. 6
to 25. 
33) In the relief portion, 1/3 rd share was given of the suit schedule
property to plaintiff,  Defendant No. 1, Defendant Nos 2 to 5
respectively in the suit.  The attempt of the appellant to implead in the
final decree also failed and the appellant has been kept out of the final
decree proceedings.  
34) In the background of this finding, for the writ appellate court in
the impugned order to conclude, as it did in para 9 (Supra), that “a
competent court of law has already adjudicated the claim of the
appellant” cannot be justified.  On merits, we find the holding of the
learned Single Judge, that the respondent settlor J. Ramakrishnan
herein, who was the writ petitioner is at liberty to pursue remedy in
the competent court of law was justified. On facts, if the appellant so
desires, is at liberty to pursue such other civil remedy as open to him,
if it otherwise maintainable in law.  All that we are inclined to
25

## Page 171

conclude is that in the teeth of the facts as narrated above, it could not
be said that the Block Development Officer was not justified in
objecting and the sub-registrar was not justified in giving a check slip.
All these disputed facts could not have been gone into by the sub-
registrar.
35) The writ court also could not have adjudicated the disputed
questions of fact.
36) In the teeth of these findings, we are of the opinion that the
Division Bench clearly erred in finding in paragraph 9 that there were
conclusive holdings against the appellant insofar as their claim over
the property was concerned. The appellant herein claims title to the
property to the extent of 1.25 acres of the total extent (undivided) by
virtue of a Gift Deed dated 13.12.1976.
37) Under these circumstances, we have no hesitation in holding
that the Division Bench ought not to have set aside the judgment of
the learned Single Judge.  We set aside the judgment dated
20.03.2024 of the Division Bench of the High Court and restore the
judgment dated 11.07.2023 of the learned Single Judge.  Parties are at
liberty to pursue their civil remedies which will be decided in
26

## Page 172

accordance with law, uninfluenced by either the judgment of the
learned Single Judge in the writ petition and the Division Bench in
the writ appeal or the present judgment.
38) The Civil Appeal is allowed in the above terms. No order as to
costs.

4. It is a matter of record that protests were held between
20.07.2026 and 25.07.2026 in Delhi and in different areas of the
applicant-States as well as other parts of the country in which
thousands of young students participated. As a sequel to these
protests, 13 FIRs, details whereof have been reproduced above, came
to be filed by the Delhi Police in different police stations.
Similarly, several FIRs, as reproduced above, were also filed in
different police stations across the applicant-States. 
5.   As a gesture of goodwill and to ensure that the subject FIRs
do not cause any prejudice to the young students who participated
in the peaceful protests, and also as an acknowledgement of the
fact that mere participation in the protests is not taken as an
offence under the penal laws, the Central Government and the
15

## Page 189

applicant-States have taken a conscious decision not to pursue the
above-enumerated FIRs registered against the protesters.
6. A further commitment has been made that if any other FIR is
found to have been registered with regard to the same incident(s),
as  mentioned  in  the  subject  FIRs,  the  Delhi  Police  or  the
applicant-States  shall  not  oppose  the  affected  party  seeking
similar relief from this Court, namely, the quashing of such FIRs.
Learned Solicitor General, on instructions, has further submitted
that no fresh FIR qua the incidents of protests between 20/07/2026
and 25/07/2026 shall be registered in Delhi or in any other part of
the country.
7. As already noted, the Delhi Police has, in its application,
carved out an exception with respect to 2873 individuals allegedly
having serious criminal antecedents as per the National Crime
Records Bureau database and who were prima  facie  reported to be
present at the protest site. It is averred that an investigation is
required to ascertain the commission of offences relating to (i)
bodily harm or (ii) destruction of public property. Accordingly,
the Delhi Police has sought leave of this Court to register a fresh
FIR only against these 2873 individuals and that too, in conformity
with the observations made by this Court in its order dated
03/08/2026, wherein it was clarified that no protection could be
afforded to persons having criminal antecedents of ‘grave and
heinous offences’.
8. It is in this backdrop that the applicants, namely, the Delhi
Police and the four States, have sought the invocation of the
powers of this Court under Article 142 of the Constitution to quash
16

## Page 190

the subject FIRs, as per the details given in paragraph 3,
reproduced above.
9. During the course of hearing, the learned Solicitor General of
India has fairly stated that there may be more FIRs in the States
and Union Territories other than the applicant-States pertaining to
the same incidents of protests. He has submitted that it may be
advisable to put an end to those FIRs too. He has accordingly
sought appropriate directions from this Court for the closure of
those FIRs as well.
10. As regards the grant of compensation to the families of the
victim students, who committed suicide in connection with the
National Eligibility-cum-Entrance Test (NEET) UG examination, 2026,
learned Solicitor General of India states that the students who
committed suicide would be situated in different parts of the
Country.  Accordingly,  there  has  to  be  a  pan-India  policy,
acceptable to the respective State Governments, for payment of
compensation to the families of such unfortunate students who
committed suicide in connection with NEET-UG examination, 2026. He
further states that the Central Government shall formulate a
policy/arrangement in consultation with the State Governments for
payment of compensation to the families of the students who
committed suicide in connection with NEET-UG examination, 2026
within 90 days and shall arrange to make the payment thereafter.
11. Meanwhile, Mr. Saurav Das, Co-convenor of the Cockroach Janta
Party (CJP), who is also present in Court, has made the following
statement:
17

## Page 191

“As Co-convenor of the Cockroach Janta Party, I want to
state that in view of the positive assurances of the
Government of India and the judicial sanctity bestowed
upon them today, and in view of the Order being passed
by this Hon’ble Court, the CJP deems it appropriate to
withdraw the call for the march on 5 th September and
looks forward to the compliance of today’s order.
I also thank the Court for this decision and the
learned counsels on both sides, Ms. Vrinda Grover and
the Solicitor General for their efforts.”
12. We have heard learned Solicitor General of India as well as
learned senior counsel/counsel for the parties and taken note of
the statement made by the Co-convenor of the CJP. In light of the
commitment made before us by all stakeholders involved, including
the Union of India, some of the State Governments and the Co-
convenor of the CJP, and most importantly, keeping in view the
future prospects of the young protesters, who bonafidely came to
participate in a peaceful protest to raise their voice in favour of
certain demands, we find it a fit case to invoke our powers under
Article 142 of the Constitution in order to do complete justice
between the parties.
13. Consequently, these applications are allowed in terms of the
following directions:
(i)  All  the  FIRs,  the  description  whereof  is  reproduced  in
paragraph 3 above, are hereby quashed along with any proceedings
arising therefrom.
(ii)  If there is any other FIR registered with respect to the same
incidents of protests between 20.07.2026 and 25.07.2026 in any of
the States/Union Territories, including non-applicant States/Union
18

## Page 192

Territories, which has not been formally brought to our notice, the
same shall not be pursued or investigated, and such FIRs shall be
taken to have been closed for all intents and purposes.
(iii)  No State/Union Territory shall register any fresh FIR in
relation  to  the  incident  of  protests  between  20.07.2026  and
25.07.2026, save and except as permitted hereinbelow.
(iv)  The Central Government/Delhi Police shall be at liberty to
register a fresh FIR with respect to the 2873 individuals as
described in paragraph 4 of its application. Needless to say that
such FIR shall be registered without prejudice to the rights of the
affected parties to take lawful recourse in accordance with law.
(v)  The Central Government, in consultation with the State
Governments/Union  Territories,  is  directed  to  formulate  the
policy/make  arrangement  on  a  pan-India  basis  for  payment  of
compensation to the families of the students who unfortunately
committed suicide in connection with the NEET-UG examination, 2026
within 90 days and shall arrange to make the payment without any
delay.  Such a policy or arrangement may then also be adopted by
all the State Governments and the Union Territories as a regular
mechanism of compensatory measures.  
14. In light of the aforesaid directions, we direct that both
sides shall honour the statements and commitments made before this
Court. We make it clear that invocation of the extraordinary powers
under Article 142 of the Constitution is subject to the condition
that both sides shall abide by the terms/understanding of mutual
settlement.

15. Since these directions are being issued in the peculiar facts
and circumstances of the case, the same shall not be taken as a

Petitioner(s), and the leaders of the CJP for their constructive
and cooperative approach, which has ensured that the best interests
of the young students remain at the forefront and that their future
is duly protected and secured.

ORDER
1. These Writ Petitions arise in the common context of several incidents
involving publication and dissemination of offending and demeaning
speech through internet-based streaming platforms. However, we find it
apposite to first refer to the different cases separately.
Page 1 of 13

## Page 195

A. CRIMINAL WRIT PETITIONS  
2. Writ Petition (Criminal) No. 83/2025 and Writ Petition (Criminal) No.
85/2025 (Criminal Writ Petitions ) arise from a common incident of
allegedly obscene comments and expressions which were circulated as
part of a comedy series published on the internet. Criminal complaints
were filed across the country, and three FIRs were lodged against the
Petitioners, as also other persons, in different States. The Petitioners,
thus, moved the Criminal Writ Petitions seeking, inter alia, quashing of
the FIRs/complaints, interim protection from arrest, or clubbing of the
various FIRs into a singular investigation.
3. In the course of hearing in these cases, this Court had granted the
Petitioner in the Writ Petition (Criminal) No. 83/2025 interim protection
from arrest, subject to depositing his passport and not airing any
further show on YouTube or other media and had also directed that no
further FIR be registered re: that incident. These conditions were
subsequently relaxed  vide orders dt. 03.03.2025 and 28.04.2025,
whereby the Petitioner was allowed to resume the production and
streaming of his show on public social media and to seek the release of
his passport from the investigating agency, i.e., the Maharashtra Cyber
Crime Bureau.
4. Additionally, this Court had observed that it would be inclined to
consider the steps taken by the State to regulate obscene speech
published on social media and digital platforms.
Page 2 of 13

## Page 196

B. CIVIL WRIT PETITION  
5. On the other hand, Writ Petition (Civil) No. 460/2025 ( Civil  Writ
Petition) was filed by an NGO engaged in social service activities
involving persons afflicted with Spinal Muscular Atrophy ( SMA), a
genetic condition which leads to muscle weakness and consequential
wasting. The Petitioner-NGO was prompted to approach this Court in
the wake of several videos being streamed over the internet, containing
content and speech which was demeaning to persons with disabilities,
including those suffering from SMA. In the said petition, the Petitioner-
NGO had also impleaded five comedians, who were found to be involved
in content over the internet which disparaged disability-afflicted
persons, as Respondent Nos. 6 to 10.
6. We may note, at this stage, that some of the private Respondents
impleaded in this petition were also accused in the FIRs forming the
foundation of the Criminal Writ Petitions.
7. Considering the gravity of the expressions disseminated by Respondent
Nos. 6 to 10 and their potential impact on the dignity of persons with
disability in contemporary society, this Court had mandated their
physical presence for the hearing of the matter. However, after they
submitted unconditional apologies, on record as well as through their
social media channels, that requirement was relaxed vide order dated
25.08.2025. Through subsequent orders, the said Respondents were
permitted to show their bona fide repentance in the shape of events
aimed at raising funds for the benefit of persons with disability, while
Page 3 of 13

## Page 197

Ms. Aparajita Singh, learned senior counsel representing the Petitioner-
NGO, had suggested that a dedicated corpus of funds ought to be
created for financial aid and assistance for people suffering from SMA.
8. Since then, the private Respondents have filed various affidavits,
statedly in compliance with the successive orders of this Court. When
the matter came up for hearing recently, we had an occasion to
consider their purported compliance and the consequential conduct.
The said conduct was, however, found to be patently lacking bona fides
on the part of Respondent Nos. 6 to 10, and  vide order dated
14.07.2026, we were constrained to impose costs amounting to a total
of Rs. 15 lakhs. We are informed that the costs have since been
deposited with the Registry of this Court.
9. Now, Respondent Nos. 6 to 10 have submitted their fresh compliance
affidavits, wherein the following steps have been highlighted:
9.1. Numerous events, with a minimum of two per month, were organised
by Respondent Nos. 6 to 10 to raise funds towards and promote
awareness regarding SMA warriors. The persons with disability,
including those suffering from SMA, were invited as guests as well as
participants, and they were also invited for special interaction with the
performers. Although ten such programmes could be organised initially,
due to logistical issues, specific arrangements could not be made for
inviting and seating specially-abled persons in four subsequently
scheduled shows. These shows are said to have been held, and the
Page 4 of 13

## Page 198

revenue generated therefrom has been earmarked for fundraising
purposes.
9.2. From the above programmes, a corpus of approximately Rs. 12.55
lakhs is said to have been created. A part of this amount has already
been donated to the Petitioner-NGO, and the private Respondents have
expressed their willingness and eagerness to similarly donate the
remaining corpus as well.
9.3. A Chess tournament for differently abled persons, named ‘Super Heroes
Cup’, was organised from 14.03.2026 to 16.03.2026 in Pune. The
tournament received widespread coverage in print and digital media,
leading to awareness being spread about various disabilities, including
SMA. The event also encouraged large donations to organisations
supporting such persons. The said event was organised through Chess
Base India, which also sponsored food, lodging, and travel for the
participants and their family, caretaker, etc. Additionally, Grandmaster
P. Harikrishna was also invited to encourage persons to participate and
to spread awareness on various disability-related issues.
9.4. Constructive conversations have taken place between Respondent Nos.
6 to 10 and the Petitioner-NGO for hosting a specialised programme
aimed at spreading awareness about SMA. They have discussed the
structure and material for such programmes to celebrate the lives of
SMA warriors. Apart from providing detailed information and sharing
ideas, the above-mentioned Respondents have expressed their gratitude
for the Petitioner-NGO's guidance in developing their programme. They
Page 5 of 13

## Page 199

are also in the process of obtaining the consent of the SMA warriors for
participation and involvement in the proposed programme.
10. These developments, which have been acknowledged by learned senior
counsel for the Petitioner-NGO, indicate true compliance with what has
been observed by this Court in previous orders. We expect that
Respondent Nos. 6 to 10 will work hard and continue on their
endeavour to organise events for celebrating the lives and enhancing
the dignity of SMA warriors. They shall also continue to seek guidance
from the Petitioner-NGO for such events as well as show promptness in
supporting any further events or initiatives suggested by the Petitioner.
11. Ms. Madhavi Diwan, learned senior counsel representing the private
Respondents, has brought a demand draft, drawn in the name of the
Registry of this Court, to enable the said Respondents to donate the
remaining corpus generated by them. Upon our persuasion, the
Petitioner-NGO has consented to accept the specified amount for
application towards one of the causes to which the NGO is dedicated.
12. Similarly, the costs deposited by Respondent Nos. 6 to 10 shall also be
transferred to the Petitioner-NGO, for being applied towards its noble
cause.
C. FINDINGS AND CONCLUDING DIRECTIONS  
13. In view of the observations made above, especially the substantial
compliance with the orders of this Court, we believe it is appropriate
Page 6 of 13

## Page 200

that the complaint(s), if any, filed against Respondent Nos. 6 to 10 in
Writ Petition (Civil) No. 460/2025 ought to be deemed as concluded.
14. At this stage, we also find it apposite that the proceedings forming the
subject matter of Writ Petition (Criminal) Nos. 83/2025 and 85/2025
be closed. The continuation of those proceedings, in the peculiar facts
and circumstances of these cases, would not serve any cogent purpose.
15. We are cognisant that important larger issues regarding the scope of
regulation of speech on internet-based social media remain to be dealt
with. In our considered opinion, those issues can be taken up by this
Court in another appropriate case, while the Criminal Writ Petitions
can be disposed of. It, however, goes without saying that there is no
impediment for the appropriate executive authority to take necessary
steps, as permissible in law, on this aspect.
16. Similarly, further hearing and judicial intervention may be required on
the suggestion by Ms. Aparajita Singh that a specialised corpus of
funds be created by the Union of India for SMA patients. She points out
that preventative as well as post-atrophy treatment is hindered due to
lack of adequate and systematic financial support. We believe that the
genesis of these Writ Petitions would not be the suitable foundation for
such consideration. It would, rather, be in the interest of justice and all
stakeholders that a dedicated case to consider this prayer be registered,
while closing the Civil Writ Petition.
17. Hence, invoking the powers vested in this Court under Article 142 of
the Constitution, we pass the following directions:

1. We have heard the learned Senior counsel appearing
for the appellant(s) and the learned ASG appearing for

2. The  disputed  property  originally  belonged  to
Indequip Engineering Company, the appellant in Civil
Appeal No. 8439 of 2013 (hereinafter referred to as, “the
Company”). Upon the coming into force of the Urban Land
(Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976 (hereinafter referred
to as,“the Act”), the Company filed a statement under
Section 6 of the Act declaring its landholding. 
3. During the pendency of the proceedings, the Company
obtained permission to mortgage the land in favour of the
Bank of India, pursuant to which the land was mortgaged.
The Bank subsequently instituted a suit for recovery of
its dues amounting to 11.50 crores. Thereafter, the₹

## Page 208

2

the Act declaring 47,374 square metres of land as excess
vacant land. The appeals preferred by the Company and the
Bank under Section 33 of the Act were dismissed by the
Urban  Land  Tribunal  (hereinafter  referred  to  as,
“Tribunal”). 
4. Subsequently, a notification under Section 10(3)
was issued, followed by a notice under Section 10(5) for
taking  possession  of  the  excess  vacant  land.  As
possession  was  not  voluntarily  surrendered,  the

(ii) AP Electrical Equipment Corp. v. Tehsildar –  2025
SCC OnLine 447;
(iii) Gajanan Kamlya Patil v. Addl. Collector & Competent
Authority – (2014) 12 SCC 523;
(iv) State U.P. v. Hari Ram (2013) 4 SCC 280;

## Page 210

4
(v) Avanti Organisation, Rajkot v. Additional Collector &
Competent Authority, Urban Land Ceiling, Rajkot  – 1988
SCC OnLine Guj 107;
(vi) Katya Co-Operative Building Society Limited & Ors.
v. The Government of Andhra Pradesh – AIR 1985 AP 242.
9. Learned counsel appearing for the respondent(s) on
the other hand would submit that the appeals are not
maintainable on two grounds. Firstly, the main appellant
before us can, at best, claim the status of a mortgagee,
being an assignee of the Bank, who was the mortgagee. The
fact that permission had earlier been granted by the
authorities to create  the mortgage does not enure to the
benefit  of  the  main  appellant.  Secondly,  the  legal
possession of the excess vacant land was duly taken. The
record  pertaining  to  the  building  situated  on  the
disputed land was prepared subsequently and was illegal.
In  any  event,  that  would  not  render  the  Panchnama
invalid, as under the Act, only possession of the excess
vacant land is required to be taken. It was further
submitted  that  there  is  no  requirement  to  issue  a
separate notice under Section 10(6) of the Act, as the
notice issued under Section 10(5) of the Act itself
clearly indicates the consequence of failure to surrender
the possession of the land to the Government or any
person authorised by the Government. 
10. The learned Counsel appearing for the Respondent
also submitted that the earlier proceedings under Section

## Page 211

5
33 of the Act would operate as res judicata against the
Bank, the predecessor-in-interest of the main appellant,
since it did not prefer any appeal against the order
passed by the Tribunal. It was, therefore, contended that
no interference is warranted, particularly when both the
Courts have concurrently held against the appellant(s).
It was further submitted that the main appellant had not
independently challenged the Tribunal’s order and was
impleaded only as a respondent in the Special Civil
Application filed by the Company, the erstwhile land
owner, which itself  chose not to file any intra-Court
appeal before the High Court.
11. On  perusal  of  the  records  and  the  statutory
provisions, we are not inclined to hold that section
10(6) of the Act,  per se , mandates the issuance of a
separate notice. We have also perused the notice under
Section 10(5) of the Act, which is a comprehensive
notice. This notice clearly stipulates the requirement of
handing over possession and the consequences that would
follow in the event of failure to surrender possession.
The finding on record is that the said notice was duly
served.  As  stated  Section  10(6)  of  the  Act  only
facilitates the Urban Land Ceiling Authority to take
possession in the event of non-compliance with the notice
issued under Section 10(5) of the Act.  It does not
mandate the issuance of a fresh notice before action is
taken under Section 10(6) of the Act. In other words, the

## Page 212

6
statutory scheme primarily contemplates the taking over
of possession of the excess vacant land, which, according
to the record, has been done in the present case.
12. There is no difficulty in holding that it is for
the authorities to satisfy the Court that, pursuant to
the Panchnama drawn, the possession has been taken.
However, we are inclined to hold that the right of the
main  appellant  is  rather  restricted  in  nature.
Furthermore,  the  main  appellant’s  predecessor-in-
interest,namely, the Bank, did not file the Special Civil
Application challenging the order passed by the Tribunal
and was only arrayed as a respondent in the Special Civil
Application filed by the Company. The Company, in turn,
did not file the intra-court appeal against the judgment
of the learned Single Judge dismissing the Special Civil
Application. The learned Single Judge has specifically
noted that the Company had abandoned the litigation and
had shown no active interest in pursuing it. Thereafter,
the Company chose to file the present appeal directly
before us. However, none has appeared on its behalf. We
have  also  been  informed  that  the  Company  is  under
liquidation. Perhaps that is the reason why it has chosen
not to pursue the present litigation before us.
13. Merely because permission was granted to create the
mortgage does not enure to the benefits of the main
appellant. In other words, what the main appellant seeks
before us is an order extending to it the benefits

## Page 213

7
available under Sections 3 and 4 of the Act. It is for the
Company, the erstwhile landowner, to make such a claim.
The proceedings before the Civil Court, to which the
respondent(s) are not parties, would not enure to the
benefit of the main appellant. As stated earlier, we are
concerned only with the possession of the excess vacant
land.
14. The other contention regarding the panchnama also
does not hold good, as it is for the Company, the
erstwhile  landowner,  to  raise  the  appropriate  plea.
Having found that the notice issued under Section 10(5)
of the Act was duly served, and that it clearly indicated
the consequential action that would follow upon failure
to surrender possession of the land, it is too late in
the day to permit the main appellant to raise all such
contentions on merits before us. Suffice it to state that
the main appellant is merely an assignee of the erstwhile
Bank, in whose favour the property in question had been
mortgaged.
15. Accordingly, we are inclined to hold that the
judgments relied upon by the learned counsel appearing
for the appellant(s), in our considered view, do not have
any bearing on the facts of the case.
16. Taking  note  of  the  facts  and  circumstances
governing the case, we have no hesitation in holding that
the order passed by the Division Bench under challenge
deserves to be affirmed, particularly when no intra-court

## Page 214

8
appeal was filed by the Company, the erstwhile landowner.
The main appellant before us also did not choose to
challenge the proceedings by filing a Special Civil
Application; instead, it preferred an intra-court appeal
against the order passed in the Special Civil Application
filed by the Company. Additionally, we take note of the
fact  that  the  predecessor-in-interest  of  the  main
appellant had invoked Section 33 of the Act, whereupon
the  Tribunal  held  that  it  had  no  locus  standi to
challenge the proceedings. The said order has attained
finality as against the predecessor of the main appellant
and is, therefore, binding upon the main appellant. In
other words, the main appellant continues to be merely a
mortgagee and, therefore, its rights are circumscribed by
the law governing mortgage alone.
17. We are conscious of the fact that we are dealing with
a very hard case. As recorded by us, there was an element
of lack of due diligence on the part of the predecessor
of the main appellant in obtaining prior permission from
the authorities before executing the deed of mortgage.
Apart from the substantial dues payable to the main
appellant, we are also confronted with the competing
interests of the erstwhile employees.
18. In such view of the matter, we grant liberty to the
main appellant, the Company, its erstwhile employees
including respondent No.8 in Civil Appeal No.8439/2013,
Rashtriya Majdoor Sangh to make a representation to

## Page 215

9
respondent No.1-State, seeking release of the specific
portion of the land declared as surplus, which may
include the constructed portion as well.
19.  We make it clear that we have not expressed any
opinion on the subsequent action of the Bank in bringing
the property to sale, as the same gives rise to a
separate cause of action.
20.  Accordingly, the appeals stand dismissed.  No costs.
21.   Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.
………………………………………….J.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
IA No.135967/2026
1. This application has been filed by Dr. Navpreet Kaur – Co-
founder of Laxmi Foundation to intervene and assist this Court in
these proceedings.  
2. Learned counsel for the applicant states that he may be
permitted to withdraw this application as he has filed a separate
I.A. (vide E-filing No.EA-SCIN01-19205-2026) seeking impleadment of
another NGO – Navya Centre for Justice and Social Change, through
its founder (Dr. Navpreet Kaur).  
3. In view of the above submission, the application is dismissed
as withdrawn.
7

## Page 235

Main Matter
4. While issuing notice, this Court had directed the Registrar
General of all the High Courts to furnish the details of pending
trials in the cases of acid attack victims in their respective
jurisdictions.  It  was  thereafter  noted  in  our  order  dated
27.01.2026 that 17 High Courts had sent their responses, the
details whereof were also mentioned in the said order.
5. While directing the High Courts to expedite the conclusion of
trials in the acid attack cases, this Court also directed the State
Governments and the concerned authorities to consider and formulate
appropriate rehabilitation measures for victims of acid attacks.
Consequently, the State Legal Services Authorities were directed to
submit  a  report  with  respect  to  the  rehabilitation  schemes
implemented by them for the grant of compensation, rehabilitation
and medical aid to the victims of acid attack.
6. In addition, the States and Union Territories were directed to
furnish information with respect to (i) the reported incidents of
acid attacks in year-wise format; (ii) whether the charge-sheets in
those cases were filed; and (iii) the number of cases still pending
at the trial stage or at the appellate stage. 
7. Another  important  direction  issued  was  to  furnish  brief
particulars of each of the victims of the acid attacks with
reference to their academic qualifications, current employment
status, marital status, and the medical treatment needed by them,
including the expenditure incurred thereon by such victims.  
8. On  09.03.2026,  the  reports  received  from  various  State
8

## Page 236

Governments and the High Courts were taken note of. Similarly, the
reports sent by the State Legal Services Authorities regarding the
victim compensation schemes and rehabilitation schemes were also
briefly referred to, whereupon a show cause notice was issued to
the State Governments and Union Territories as to why a scheme for
rehabilitation through employment in Government or Government-
controlled sectors for victims of acid attacks should not be
directed to be formulated. The State Governments were further
directed to consider a proposal to pay an honorarium equivalent to
a subsistence allowance to victims of acid attacks.
9. Some of the States have filed compliance affidavits from time
to time. We request learned counsel for both sides, along with the
learned  Amicus  Curiae , to collate the information regarding the
above issues from the compliance affidavits filed by the State
Governments and the High Courts in a tabulated form, specifically
pointing out as to whether the State Governments have introduced
any  rehabilitation  scheme  which,  inter-alia,  ensures  social
security for the victims of acid attacks. Such schemes may be
widened  to  include  free  education  at  all  levels,  employment
prospects,  free  treatment,  honorarium  during  the  period  of
unemployment, etc.  
10. Since it is not discernible from the compliance affidavit(s)
as to whether such schemes are in force, we direct all the State
Governments and the Union Territories to specifically formulate a
scheme in this regard and place the same on record within six
weeks.
11. The Union of India may also consider the desirability of
9

## Page 237

circulating a model scheme, along with a provision of necessary
assistance to the State Governments, to give effect to the above-
proposed scheme.  
12. The other challenge highlighted before this Court pertains to
the retail sale of the acid in the market. We are informed that
some guidelines were laid down in the year 2013, which have more or
less become obsolete and are not being followed. That being so, we
direct the Union of India to submit its response as to why a
complete ban on the retail sale of acid should not be imposed, or
in the alternative, why such sale should not be permitted in a very
restricted manner. Let such response be filed within six weeks.  
13. It is made clear that appropriate directions in this regard
shall be issued by us on the next date of hearing.
14. The NGOs that have come forward to assist this Court may also
submit their suggestions/recommendations, especially with respect
to any additional material that ought to be introduced in the
curriculum at the school and college levels for spreading awareness
regarding  preventative  measures  as  well  as  the  post-accident
treatments which are required on an emergency basis. Let such
suggestions also be placed on record within six weeks.
15. Post this matter for further consideration on 27.10.2026.  
(NITIN TALREJA)                           (PREETHI DILEEP KUMAR)
ASTT. REGISTRAR-cum-PS                        DY. REGISTRAR

                             O R D E R
SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CIVIL) NO. 1745 OF 2024:
Heard Mr. Vipin Sanghi, learned Senior Counsel for
the petitioners and Mr. Huzefa Aziz Ahmadi, learned
Senior Counsel for the respondent at length.
2.  At the outset, a preliminary objection was raised by
7

## Page 245

SLP (C) NO.1258/2024
learned Senior Counsel for the respondent that before the
High Court a categorical stand was taken on behalf of the
petitioners herein and the learned Single Judge of the
High Court has recorded that the learned counsel for the
respondent  (petitioners  herein)  fairly  submits  “that
there is no distinction between the set of employees in
whose favour the matter has attained finality up to the
Hon’ble Supreme Court and the present petitioners.”. It
has further been noted that such statement was based on a
communication  by  the  Petitioner-University  to  its
counsel. The order referred to of this Court was passed
in Civil Appeal Nos.2096-2198 of 2022, titled “ Jai Narain
Vyas University, Jodhpur and Anr. vs. Mukesh Sharma Etc.
Etc.”, dated 28.03.2022.
3. Learned Senior Counsel for the petitioners cannot
dispute the aforesaid recorded fact. However, he tried to
distinguish it on the ground that such is not the correct
factual position.
4. Having considered the matter, we find that it is too
late in the day for the petitioners to take a u-turn on
factual aspects, more so, when the same has attained
finality and has never been objected to either before the
High Court, or even a point taken in the pleadings in the
present case. In this connection, we refer to a decision
of  this  Court  in  State  of  Maharashtra  vs.  Ramdas
8

## Page 246

SLP (C) NO.1258/2024
Shrinivas  Nayak  and  Anr.  [(1982) 2 SCC 463], relevant
being at Paragraphs No. 4 to 8.
5. Accordingly,  the  Special  Leave  Petition  stands
dismissed.
6. However, to be fair to the petitioners we restrict
the relief granted of back wages for three years to the
respondent as has been granted by this Court in the order
dated 28.03.2022 in Civil Appeal Nos.2096-2198 of 2022.
7. After the order was dictated, learned senior counsel
for the petitioners submitted that as per the direction
of this Court in its order dated 28.03.2022, though back
wages to the respondents has been limited to three years,
but, it was his contention that some of the respondents
had chosen to move to the newly created University upon
its bifurcation from the present University and have
worked there and have got wages for such period.
8. Having regard to the aforesaid, we clarify that if
any of the respondents have worked for a period of three
years immediately before the benefit which has to accrue
as per the order of this Court dated 28.03.2022, whatever
pay/wages/allowances they may have received shall be
adjusted from the liability of the petitioner-University
while making payment to them in terms of the said order.
9. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

bullet.

1. Leave granted. 
2. Heard learned counsel for the parties.  
3. The Respondent approached the Appellant to purchase maize 
and soybean seeds worth Rs. 5,00,000/ -. To discharge this 
sale consideration, the Respondent issued a cheque dated 
16.05.2016. Upon presentation by the Appellant on 18.07.2016, 
the cheque was returned dishonored , with the bank's 
endorsement "stop payment instruction". 
4. Despite receiving a legal notice demanding payment, the 
respondent failed to pay and instead issued a reply denying 
any liability, prompting the Appellant to file a private 
complaint under Section 200 of the C ode of Criminal 
Procedure, 1973 for an offence punishable under Section 138 

## Page 274

2 
of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (“The Act”). 
5. The other appeals are in similar circumstances, but the case 
details are set out hereunder for clarity:

6. On the evidence, the learned Civil Judge and JMFC, Hukkeri, 
convicted the respondent on 20.02.2021 and sentenced him to 
six months of simple imprisonment and a fine of 
Rs.5,05,000/-. Aggrieved by the conviction, the respondent 
filed a criminal appeal before the Court of the VII 
Additional District and Sessions Judge, Belagavi. By an order 
dated 09.11.2021, the First Appellate Court dismissed the 
appeal and confirmed the judgment and sentence of the Trial 
Court. The respondent then moved the High Court of Karnataka, 
Dharwad Bench (“High Court”), by a criminal revision petition 
seeking acquittal. 
7. The High Court partly allowed the Respondent's revision 
petition by modifying his sentence for a conviction under 

## Page 275

3 
Section 138 of the Act. It determined that while the findings 
of guilt were based on legal evidence, the original 
imposition of six months of simple imprisonment was 
unwarranted. Consequently, the High Court set aside the 
sentence of imprisonment and instead ordered the respondent 
to pay only the fine amount, along with a default sentence. 
8. Hence the Appeal(s). The impugned Judgment has confirmed the 
conviction but, at sentencing, has limited the remedy to 
compensation. The learned counsel for the Appellant(s) argues 
that non-payment of sufficient compensation to farmers is 
illegal and amounts to excessive indulgence toward a 
defaulter.  
9. The learned counsel for the respondent contends that the High 
Court properly exercised its discretion in the impugned 
Judgment and that no interference is warranted.  
10. Considering the facts and circumstances of the case, 
specifically that the underlying transactions involve a 
failure to clear long -standing dues owed to farmers for 
agricultural produce since 2016, this Court is of the view 
that substantial legal justice must balance punitive severity 
with financial restitution to the aggrieved payees/farmers. 
Section 138 of the Act provides a regulatory remedy that 
enables the calculation of fines up to twice the face value 
of the dishonored instrument. 
11. Accordingly, to give effect to Section 138 of the Act  in 
letter and spirit  and to ensure equitable financial 
restitution, this Court deems it fit to enhance the

compensation awarded to the Appellants. Consequently, the 
Respondent is directed to pay the enhanced compensation/fine

2. Being  aggrieved  by  the  judgement  and  order  dated
22.04.2026 passed by the High Court of Karnataka at Bengaluru
in Criminal Revision Petition No.336 of 2018, the appellant
herein has preferred the present appeal.
3. Briefly  stated,  the  facts  of  the  case  are  that  on
15.04.2014,  the  deceased,  while  riding  motorcycle  bearing
registration No. KA-14/Y-1911 with PW-2 as pillion rider, met
with an accident involving a lorry bearing registration No. KA-
02/AA-4191 near Untoorukatte Kaimara that was being driven by
the appellant herein. It was alleged that the appellant was
driving the said lorry in a rash and negligent manner, as a
result whereof the rider sustained fatal injuries and succumbed
to the same at the spot, while the pillion rider suffered
grievous injuries. On the basis of a complaint lodged by the
brother-in-law of the deceased, proceedings were initiated
against the appellant for offences punishable under Sections
1

## Page 288

279, 338 and 304A of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (“IPC”, for
short) and Sections 134(a) and 134(b) of the Motor Vehicles
Act, 1988 (“MV Act”, for short).
3.1 By judgement and order dated 25.04.2017, the Court of the
Senior  Civil  Judge  and  Judicial  Magistrate  First  Class,
Thirthahalli  in  Criminal  Case  No.328/2016  convicted  the
appellant for the aforesaid offences and thereby sentenced him
to undergo simple imprisonment for six months for the offence
under Section 304A of the IPC along with fine amount of
Rs.5000/- and simple imprisonment for one month for the offence
under Sections 134(a) and 134(b) of the MV Act along with fine
of Rs.500/-. Aggrieved, by the order dated 25.04.2017, the
appellant preferred Criminal Appeal No. 42 of 2017 which came
to  be  dismissed  by  the  III  Additional  Sessions  Judge,
Shivamogga vide judgement dated 02.03.2018 and thereby upheld
and confirmed the judgment of conviction and order of sentence
passed by the Court of the Senior Civil Judge and Judicial
Magistrate First Class, Thirthahalli.
3.2 Aggrieved by the concurrent findings of the Courts below,
the appellant preferred Criminal Revision Petition No. 336 of
2018 before the High Court of Karnataka at Bengaluru. The High
Court, vide impugned judgement dated 22.04.2026, dismissed the
revision petition and affirmed the conviction and sentence,
holding, inter alia, that the testimony of PW-6, coupled with
the evidence of the injured witness (PW-2) and the spot
mahazar, sufficiently established the prosecution case. The
2

## Page 289

High Court further observed that PW-6 had not been cross-
examined by the defence and, therefore, his testimony remained
uncontroverted insofar as the identity of the driver was
concerned.
3.3 Being aggrieved by the impugned judgment and order of the
High Court of Karnataka dated 22.04.2026 in Criminal Revision
Petition No. 336 of 2018, the appellant has preferred the
present appeal.
4. We have heard learned counsel for the appellant and
learned Additional Advocate General for the respondent-State.
We have also perused the material on record.
5. Learned counsel for the appellant submitted that for the
purpose of seeking modification in the sentence imposed on the
appellant herein, so as to convert the same into one of fine
both under Section 304-A of the IPC and Section 187 of the MV
Act, the appellant has deposited an amount of Rs.3,00,000/-
before the Trial court (Court of Senior Civil Judge and
Judicial Magistrate First Class at Thirthahalli) in Criminal
Case No.328 of 2016. In the circumstances, the punishment of
imprisonment may be set aside and converted to one of payment
of  only  fine  under  both  the  aforesaid  provisions  and
consequently, the said amount of Rs.3,00,000/- may be paid to
the claimants being the dependants of the deceased.
6. Learned AAG appearing for the State of Karnataka submitted
that appropriate orders may be made in the case having regard
3

## Page 290

to  the  fact  that  the  appellant  has  deposited  a  sum  of
Rs.3,00,000/- before the Trial Court. 
7. Consequently, we find that the ends of justice would be
met in this case if the order of punishment with regard to the
Simple imprisonment for a period of six months and for one
month under the aforesaid two provisions i.e., Section 304-A of
the IPC and Section 187 of the MV Act, are modified and
instead, the punishment one of fine only is imposed and the
fine shall be Rs.3,00,000/- under both the aforesaid provisions
inclusive of what has been already imposed.
8. Since the said amount has already been deposited by the
appellant before the Trial Court, we direct the Trial Court to
issue notice to the claimants and take steps to pay the said
amount  to  the  claimants/dependents  of  the  deceased-
Marulasiddappa, who died in the accident that occurred on
15.04.2014 when the appellant was riding the lorry which caused
the accident.
9. This appeal is disposed of in the aforesaid terms.

2. The appeal arises from an order of the High Court
directing an FIR to be registered for investigation of a
cognizable offence under Section 289 of  Indian  Penal
Code, 1860  (IPC), thus, reversing the order of the Chief
Metropolitan Magistrate, Saket Courts, New Delhi and the
Additional Sessions Judge, South East District, Saket
Courts New Delhi finding no reason to issue such a
direction. The incident that led to the complaint before
the CMM occurred when two dogs residing with their
owners were taken out for a stroll. The complainants;
mother and daughter, were residing in D54, Ground Floor,
Defence Colony, New Delhi, while the appellant herein is
Page 1 of 4

## Page 295

said to be residing along with his parents D-361, Defence
Colony. The allegation was that while the mother and
daughter were walking their dog, the appellant’s dog,
without  a  leash,  came  from  the  opposite  direction
accompanied by a person; as per the appellant’s version,
a caretaker. Despite asking the dog to be taken away, the
man accompanying the dog kept walking towards them
and the mother and the daughter, both suffering from hip
ailments, were put in a panic situation. There was also an
allegation that the man accompanying the dog, who was
named in the complaint, was drunk and unresponsive.
Admittedly, they immediately called for help and one
Head Constable came from the Defence Colony Police
Station. The police registered a Non-Cognizable Report
(NCR) under Section 323 of the IPC.
3. The mother-daughter duo filed a complaint before
the CMM Court, improving on the complaint made before
the police. Two wound certificates were also produced.
The CMM found from the facts that no investigation is
required and it was also observed that if it is found
necessary, an enquiry under Section 202 of  Code  of
Page 2 of 4

## Page 296

Criminal  Procedure,  1973  (Cr.PC) can be initiated. The
Additional Sessions Judge agreed with the order of the
CMM. The High Court on a revision filed, however, opined
that there is a cognizable offence made out under Section
289 of the IPC and hence directed the police to register
an FIR and conduct an investigation.
4. We see from the wound certificate that the mother
suffered no injuries and the injuries suffered by the
daughter were minor abrasions on both feet; definitely,
not due to the attack of a dog. In fact, the complaint itself
is extracted by the High Court, which indicates that on
seeing the approaching dog, the duo had requested the
man accompanying the dog to take it away. The mother &
daughter also had a dog with them and there is no attack
spoken of by the other dog. The allegation of the mother
was also that the daughter was ‘almost bitten by the dog’
and  ‘the  dog  almost  jumped  on  me’.  So,  nothing
transpired as to attract Section 289 of the IPC.
5. We find absolutely no reason to sustain the order of
the High Court and we reverse the same, restoring the
order of the CMM as affirmed by the Additional Sessions
Page 3 of 4

## Page 297

Judge. Though not relevant to the issue, the appellant
also has a contention that the complaint was false and
was motivated by reason of a prior litigation between the
father of the appellant and the complainants.
6. The appeal stands allowed.
7. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

4. Ms.  Chitransha  Singh  Sikarwar,  learned
counsel appearing on behalf of respondent-State
who is on advance notice has vehemently opposed
the suspension of sentence contending inter  alia
that after full-fledged trial appellant has been
convicted based on eye-witnesses’ statements and
(  @ SLP (CRL) NO. 49762/2026)                           1

## Page 301

as such the chances of appellant’s succeeding in
appeal before High Court being remote his prayer
for suspension of sentence and grant of bail be
rejected.
5. The appellant who was tried in Sessions Trial Case
No.322 of 2016  for an offence punishable under Section
302 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (“for short IPC”) has
been convicted after full fledged trial and an appeal filed
challenging the same in Criminal Appeal No. 28/2026 is
pending  before  the  jurisdictional  High  Court.  The
application filed for suspension of sentence and grant of
bail having been negatived by the High Court by the
impugned order/judgment dated 20.4.2026, the appellant
is before this Court.
6. The gist of the prosecution case is that appellant and
deceased namely Jitu Khandare were friends and on the ill
fated day i.e., 15.03.2016 both were in an inebriated
condition and had a quarrel near Tata Capital Building at
1:00 am, which culminated in appellant assaulting the
deceased with brick and as a result of injuries sustained, he
(  @ SLP (CRL) NO. 49762/2026)                           2

## Page 302

is said to have succumbed and appellant came to be
arrested at the spot. It has been brought on record before
the trial Court that appellant had repeatedly struck the
deceased on head during the quarrel. Any examination or
scrutiny and evaluation of the evidence tendered by the
prosecution witnesses at this stage, is likely to prejudice
the  rights  of  the  parties.  It  is  no  doubt  true  that
prosecution has relied upon medical evidence reflecting 22
injuries  sustained  by  the  deceased.  We  desist  from
scrutinizing  the  said  evidence,  notwithstanding  the
attractive arguments canvassed on behalf of appellant, we
leave the same to be examined by the High Court where
the appeal is pending. Having regard to the fact that
appellant has spent 10 years in jail and there being no
criminal  antecedents  against  him  and  the  conduct
certificate issued by the jail authorities reflecting there
being no negative report, we are of the considered view
that appellant would be entitled for the suspension of
sentence.
7. Having regard to the fact that the appeal is of the
(  @ SLP (CRL) NO. 49762/2026)                           3

## Page 303

year 2026 and the consideration of the same would be time
consuming is also the ground on which also the appellant
would be entitled for suspension of sentence and grant of
bail.
8. Hence, we allow this appeal, set aside the impugned
order, direct the sentence imposed by the trial Court in
Sessions Trial Case No.322 of 2016 dated 13.12.2022
stands suspended and appellant is ordered to be released
on bail on such terms and conditions as the jurisdictional
Court deems fit to impose. Accordingly, the appeal is
allowed.
9. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

O R D E R
1. By way of these applications, the applicants have
prayed for the following relief(s):
“ a. Direct the Union Ministry of Defence to provide
the Applicant consequential pensionary benefits of her
Permanent  Commission,  computed  on  the  basis  of
completion (20) years of service, as has been done to
the other parties in the judgment of Wg. Cdr. A.U.
Tayyaba (Retd.) v. Union of India, (2023) 5 SCC 688 and
the order dated 16.09.2025 in M.A. No. 1718-1721/2024 in
the captioned Civil Appeal;
b. Alternatively, clarify that the relief with regard to
pensionary  benefits  granted  to  the  parties  in  the
judgment of Wg. Cdr. A.U. Tayyaba (Retd.) v. Union of
India, (2023) 5 SCC 688 and the order dated 16.09.2025
in M.A. No. 1718-1721/2024 in the captioned Civil Appeal
also inure to the benefit of similarly situated non-
parties;
c.  Further,  in  the  alternative,  direct  the  Union
Ministry of Defence to consider the representation of
the Applicant dated 08.10.2025 even though the Applicant
was not a party to the proceedings in Wg. Cdr. A.U.
Tayyaba (Retd.) v. Union of India, (2023) 5 SCC 688 and
the order dated 16.09.2025 in M.A. No. 1718-1721/2024 in
the captioned Civil Appeal;
d. Pass such other orders and further orders as may be
deemed necessary on the facts and in the circumstances
of the case. ”
2. We have heard Mr. Huzefa A. Ahmadi, the learned
Senior Counsel appearing on behalf of the applicants, and
1

## Page 319

Mr. Brijender Chahar, the learned Additional Solicitor
General appearing on behalf of the Union of India.
3. We take notice of the order dated 16.09.2025 in
M.A.Nos.1718-1721/2025 with M.A.Nos.1722-1725/2025 passed
in identical facts concerning the identically situated
Wing Commanders, which reads as under:
“
MISCELLANEOUS APPLICATION NOS.1718-1721/2025 (@
DIARY  NO.32025/2024)  IN  CIVIL  APPEAL  NOS.79-
82/2012
1.  Applications  seeking  permission  to  file  the
Miscellaneous Applications are granted. 
2. Delay condoned.
3. This Miscellaneous Application is at the instance of
a retired Wing Commander viz. Anupama Joshi.
4. The applicant has prayed for the following reliefs:
“a. Direct the Union Ministry of Defence to provide the
Applicant  consequential  pensionary  benefits  of  her
Permanent  Commission,  computed  on  the  basis  of
completion of 20 years of service, as has been done to
the other parties in the judgment of Wg. Cdr. A.U.
Tayyaba (Retd.) v. Union of India, (2023) 5 SCC 688 and
the order dated 15.04.2024 in M.A. Diary No. 8208/2024
in the captioned Civil Appeal; 
b. Alternatively, clarify that the relief with regard to
pensionary  benefits  granted  to  the  parties  in  the
judgment of Wg. Cdr. A.U. Tayyaba (Retd.) v. Union of
India, (2023) 5 SCC 688 and the order dated 15.04.2024
in M.A. Diary No. 8208/2024 in the captioned Civil
Appeal also inure to the benefit of similarly situated
non-parties; 
c.  Further,  in  the  alternative,  direct  the  Union
Ministry of Defence to consider the representations of
the  Applicant  dated  03.05.2023  and  17.07.2023  even
though the Applicant was not a party to the proceedings
in Wg. Cdr. A.U. Tayyaba (Retd.) v. Union of India,
(2023) 5 SCC 688 dated 16.11.2022 and the order dated
15.04.2024 in M.A. Diary No. 8208/2024 in the captioned
Civil Appeal.
d. Pass such other orders and further orders as may be
deemed necessary on the facts and in the circumstances
of the case.”
5. It appears from the materials on record that she was
2

## Page 320

released from the Indian Air Force (IAF) upon completing
15 years as a Short Service Commission Woman Officer
(SSCWO).
6. It is not in dispute that she was one of the
petitioners in the litigation that led to the Judgment
rendered in “Secretary, Ministry of Defence v. Babita
Puniya and Others”, (2020) 7 SCC 469.
7. The Union of India being aggrieved by the decision of
the Delhi High Court in Babita Puniya (supra) challenged
the same before this Court by way of Special Leave
Petition.  The  challenge  by  the  Union  was  to  the
direction issued by the High Court to grant permanent
commission to the women officers.
8. We take notice of the fact that by the time the
decision of the Delhi High Court was pronounced in
Babita  Puniya  (supra),  the  applicant  had  already
completed 15 years of service and was released.
9. It was brought to our notice that on completion of 15
years, she was offered permanent commission but the same
was declined as by that time, the applicant had already
taken up some other employment. But for the decision in
Babita Puniya (supra), she would not have been entitled
to pension having not completed 20 years of pensionable
service.
10. Later, this Court in “WG CDR A.U. Tayyaba (Retired)
and Others v. Union of India and Others”, (2023) 5 SCC
688, extended the benefit of the Judgment in Babita
Puniya (supra) rendered by this Court reported in (2020)
7 SCC 469 and “Union of India and Others v. Lieutenant
Commander Annie Nagaraja and Others” (2020) 13 SCC 1 to
identically placed SSCWOS.
11. The benefit was granted irrespective of the fact
whether the officers had completed 20 years of service
or not.
12. The Department clarified that all persons who had
completed 14 years of service would be deemed to have
completed 20 years and consequently entitled to the
pension.
13.  It  is  the  case  of  the  applicant  that  having
completed 15 years of service, she qualifies to be
deemed to have completed 20 years of service in terms of
WG CDR A.U. Tayyaba (Retired) (supra) and also being one
of the petitioners in Babita Puniya (supra).
14. While affirming the judgment of the Delhi High
Court, this Court in Para 87.3 of Babita Puniya (supra)
observed as under: “87.3. SSC women officers who are
granted PC in pursuance of the above directions will be
entitled  to  all  consequential  benefits  including
promotion  and  financial  benefits.  However,  these
3

## Page 321

benefits would be made available to those officers in
service or those who had moved the Delhi High Court by
filing the writ petitions and those who had retired
during the course of the pendency of the proceedings.”
15. Thus, the Short Service Commission Women Officers
who are granted permanent commission in pursuance of the
above directions would be entitled to all consequential
benefits  including  promotion  and  other  financial
benefits.  However,  these  benefits  would  be  made
available to those Officers in service or those who had
moved the Delhi High Court by filing writ petitions and
those who had retired during the course of the pendency
of the proceedings.
16. It is very clear that the applicant before us falls
in the later part of para 87.3, referred to above.
17. Having heard Mr. Huzefa Ahmadi, the learned Senior
counsel appearing for the applicant and Ms. Aishwarya
Bhati,  the  learned  Additional  Solicitor  General
appearing  for  the  Union  of  India,  we  allow  this
application.
18. We declare that the applicant is entitled to the
benefit of the judgment in WG CDR A.U. Tayyaba (Retired)
(supra) as also the clarificatory order dated 15-4-2024
in MA(D)8208/2024 on the ground of parity.
19. As a result, we declare that the applicant is
entitled to grant of pension computed from such date
that she would have completed 20 years of service i.e.
completion of 20 years of service.
20. We direct the Union of India to undertake the
necessary exercise for grant of pension with arrears
including all other benefits to which the applicant is
entitled to, like the benefits which have been extended
to other similarly situated Officers.
21. Let this exercise be undertaken at the earliest and
be completed within a period of three months from today
without fail.
22. In view of the aforesaid, the connected application
of Wing Commander Kartika Kilam (Retd.) is also allowed
in the aforesaid terms.
23. Pending applications, if any, also stand disposed
of. ”
4. In  the  facts  of  these  cases,  we  allow  these
applications  in  the  very  same  terms  as  the  order
aforesaid and direct the Union to undertake the necessary
exercise for grant of pension with arrears including all
4

## Page 322

other benefits to which the applicants are entitled, like
the benefits which have been extended to other similarly
situated officer(s).
5. Accordingly, the present Miscellaneous Applications
stand disposed of.
6. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.
