1. Exemption application is allowed.
2. Leave granted.
3. The present appeal arises out of the final
judgment and order dated 27.07.2026 passed by the
High Court of Punjab & Haryana at Chandigarh in
CRM-M-22526-2026,  whereby  the  bail  application
filed by the appellant in connection with FIR
No.376/2025 registered at Police Station Shahabad,
District Kurukshetra, Haryana, was rejected.
4. The appellant is an undertrial accused facing
prosecution under Sections 103(1), 3(5), 61(2),
111(2),  111(3),  111(5),  238,  and  253  of  the
Crl. Appeal _________/2026 @ SLP (Crl.) No.15247/2026 1

## Page 337

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023, along with
Sections 25 and 27 of the Arms Act, 1959.
5. It is submitted by the learned counsel for
the appellant that the appellant was not present
at the spot of the incident, nor was he attributed
any direct overt act in the principal homicidal
act. The appellant has been in continuous judicial
custody since 25.06.2025, having completed over 1
year  and  2  months  of  incarceration  as  an
undertrial  prisoner.  Investigation  qua  the
appellant stands completed, and the charge sheet
has already been filed. Several co-accused persons
facing  similar  allegations  of  facilitation,
supplying  vehicles/weapons,  and  harbouring
(including Sachin, Mohit Kumar, Dipender Pal Singh
@ Kirat, Abhishek Thukral @ Abbu, Prabhjot Singh,
Vansh Rana, Jaspal Singh, and Gaurav Gupta) have
already been enlarged on bail by the High Court.
6. The learned counsel for the State has opposed
the grant of regular bail, contending that the
appellant is part of an organised crime syndicate
Crl. Appeal _________/2026 @ SLP (Crl.) No.15247/2026 2

## Page 338

and played an active role in procuring the vehicle
and harbouring the main assailant.
7. Having considered the rival submissions, the
period of custody undergone by the appellant, the
completion of the investigation, the grant of bail
to multiple co-accused persons facing analogous
allegations, and without expressing any opinion on
the merits of the case, we are inclined to enlarge
the appellant on regular bail.
8. Accordingly, the impugned judgment and order
dated 27.07.2026 passed by the High Court of
Punjab & Haryana in CRM-M-22526-2026 is set aside.
The appellant (Ikshan Singh Mehta) is ordered to
be released on regular bail in connection with FIR
No.376/2025,  Police  Station  Shahabad,  District
Kurukshetra, subject to terms and conditions that
the trial court may deem fit and proper to impose.
The  appellant  shall  cooperate  with  the  trial
proceedings and not indulge in any crimes; failing
which, the trial court would be entitled to cancel
the bail granted.
Crl. Appeal _________/2026 @ SLP (Crl.) No.15247/2026 3

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Heard. Perused the records.
2. The present case was registered on the basis of a Vigilance Enquiry conducted
by the Police regarding property bearing E-152/A, Sainik Farms, New Delhi.
The property originally belonged to Coomar Narayan and his wife Geetanjali
Narayan; Coomar Narayan died in 2000 and Geetanjali Narayan was murdered
in 2002, following which the property remained locked and under police watch
as no legal heir or claimant came forward. During the Vigilance enquiry, Ran
Singh/Respondent No.1 claimed to have been in possession of the property
since 29.12.2005, purportedly on the basis of an arrangement with Radhika
Narayan, who claimed to be the daughter and sole legal heir of the deceased
couple.  However,  the  enquiry  revealed  that  Ran  Singh  had  not  physically
entered  the  property  before  05.02.2008,  while  Radhika  could  not  produce
authentic documents establishing her status as the legal heir. The enquiry also
disclosed contradictions in the statements of Ran Singh, Radhika Narayan and
Inder Singh, as well as discrepancies in the documents relied upon by Radhika.
It was accordingly alleged that the three had acted in connivance to fraudulently
enter and usurp the property by relying upon false/forged documents, leading to
registration of  the  FIR No.337/2008  for  the alleged  offence  under Section
448/34 of IPC.
3. Subsequent to the investigation, chargesheet has been filed for the offences
under Sections 448/453/420/468/471/120B of the IPC after a gap of 11 years
and  the  learned  Magistrate  took  cognizance  of  the  offences  under  under
Sections 448/453/120B IPC only and summoned all the accused.  The question
of taking cognizance for remaining offences was left open till filing of FSL
2

## Page 359

report by way of supplementary chargesheet.
4. The accused/Respondent No. 1 being aggrieved by the said order of taking
cognizance and summoning has filed a Criminal Revision No.124/2021 before
the Additional Sessions Judge under Section 397 of Cr.P. C. and in the said
proceedings, the petitioner filed an application for impleadment which came to
be dismissed by the Session Judge. The Revision Petition came to be allowed
and order of the learned Magistrate taking cognizance, was set aside on the
ground that it was barred by limitation under Section 468 CrPC and the matter
was remanded for fresh order on cognizance.
5. Being aggrieved by the same, the petitioner filed a Criminal Miscellaneous
Case  No.8644/2024  along  with  Criminal  Miscellaneous  Application
Nos.33075-76/2024 under Section 528 BNSS challenging the order of dismissal
of his application for impleadment and against the order of allowing of the
revision petition filed by the Respondent No. 1/Accused respectively. Criminal
Miscellaneous Application Nos.33075-76/2024 came to be rejected by the High
Court on the ground that petitioner is not having locus standi and as such
question of examining the plea of limitation on merits, was not gone into.
Parallelly they connected Criminal Miscellaneous Case No.8644/2024, under
which the order dated 15.04.2024, dismissing the petitioner's application to be
impleaded  as  a  victim  party  in  the  revision  proceedings,  which  had  been
dismissed by the learned Additional Sessions Judge, came to be dismissed on
the ground that petitioner as a third party lacks locus standi to intervene in a
State prosecution. Hence, these two Special Leave Petitions.
6. Though  several  contentions  have  been  raised  by  the  Learned  Counsels
appearing for the parties, we do not propose to go into these aspects except
observing that issue of limitation is still at large before the learned Magistrate in
view of the order of remand that has been passed  by the Sessions Judge.
3

## Page 360

Learned counsel appearing for the State would submit that an application for
condoning the delay has also been filed. As such, leaving open the question to
be examined by the learned Magistrate who shall take note of the dicta laid by
this  Court  in  the  matter  of  Gukak  Patel  Volkart  Ltd.  v.  Dundayya
Gurushiddaiah Hiremath & Ors ., reported in (1991) 2 SCC 141 we dispose of
these petitions. We request the learned Magistrate to examine the issue of
taking cognizance with reference to criminal trespass in the teeth of law laid
down by this Court and contentions of both the parties in this regard are kept
open to be urged before the learned Magistrate.
7. Though  the  learned  counsel  appearing  for  the  petitioner  has  vehemently
contended that petitioner is claiming right, title and interest over the disputed
property, being the uterine son, which is alleged to have been trespassed by the
accused persons, which is seriously disputed by Respondent No.1 appearing in
person, this Court would not embark upon conducting any inquiry in that regard
as rightly observed by the learned Sessions Judge and the High Court that the
issue relating to the legal status of the petitioner, will have to be thrashed out in
the civil proceedings and therefore would not require any further elaboration
except reiteration of the finding recorded by the Courts below. At the most, the
petitioner can be permitted to assist the prosecution in effectively in defending
the charge laid against the accused persons, if he decides to do so. It is made
clear that petitioner herein would alone be entitled to assist the prosecution and
not through any agent created through power of attorney. Except to this extent
of clarification, we do not propose to examine any other aspect.
8. Accordingly Special Leave Petitions stand disposed of.
9.  Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

O R D E R
1. Heard.
2. Leave granted.
3.  Appellant has been arraigned as an accused in FIR No.640/2025 registered
for the offences punishable under Sections 471, 468, 467, 465, 420, 409, 408,
120-B and 201 of Indian Penal Code, 1860 (IPC) and Sections 3 and 4 of the
Maharashtra Protection of Interest of Depositors (in Financial Establishments)
Act, 1999.
4. It is the case of the prosecution that a complaint came to be lodged by one
Mr.Arpit, who alleged that he and his mother had accounts with Mahila Urban
Co-operative Credit Society Ltd. since 2023 and they had fixed deposit which is
now amounting to Rs.24,45,000/-. It is further alleged that on maturity of the
said deposit, whenever the complainant and his mother went to withdraw the
money, the Society remained closed and on one of the occasion they also saw
Chairperson and when enquired for repayment, they were informed that society
do not have money. Since appellant is said to be an employee of the credit Co-
1                                                                                         SLP(CRL.) NO.14832 OF 2026

## Page 368

operative Society. Hence, the complainant approached District Deputy Registrar
(DDR) and came to know that the Credit Co-operative Society in all had
misappropriated Rs.30,78,96,676/- belonging to different persons and had
caused a financial loss to the tune of Rs.4,43,91,657/-.
5.  On investigation being taken has resulted in chargesheet being filed qua
eight accused persons only. It would emerge from the records that appellant
joined services of the Co-operative Society as a Senior Clerk in the month of
April, 2021 and he was arrested on 13.09.2025 and has been in custody till
date. The application for grant of bail sought before the trial court and High
Court came to be rejected. The role attributed to the appellant as per the
chargesheet is:  appellant was working as a clerk and his user ID was utilized in
making the transaction and appellant is said to have been involved in making
bogus term loan files. In all there are 33 accused and similarly placed accused
persons or, in other words, the allegation against the other accused, is similar to
the one made against the appellant and they had been released on either
anticipatory bail or regular bail, namely, about 16 accused persons out of 33
have been granted bail and 12 are said to be absconding and 4 persons
including the appellant are in jail. One of the accused persons has since expired.
The prosecution has cited 47 witnesses and charges having been framed on
30.06.2026 and trial is yet to commence.
6. Having regard to aforestated facts viz., appellant was working as a Senior
Clerk in the society and prosecution has to prove that appellant was executing
or implementing the instructions received from the senior officers and his
complicity in the alleged offence. At this stage, we are of the considered view
that his continued incarceration would not be warranted or, in other words, he is
entitled for being released on bail.
2                                                                                         SLP(CRL.) NO.14832 OF 2026

## Page 369

7. In fact, primary accused who are having much higher accountability, have
already been released on bail, namely, the Chairman, Secretary, Directors,
Cashier and Clerks have been granted either anticipatory bail or regular bail. In
these circumstances, we are of the considered view that appellant-Narayan is
entitled for grant of regular bail.
8. Hence, we allow the appeal and set aside the impugned order. Appellant is
ordered to be released on regular bail on such terms and conditions as the
jurisdictional Court may deem fit to impose.
9. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

cultivating  the  land  bearing  Survey  No.10/1  of  Vajarahalli
Village, Uttarahalli Hobli, Bangalore South Taluk, measuring 1
acre 4 guntas. It was represented that it was agricultural land
and that his father had planted mango trees as well as coconut
trees and they had been raising crops therein for more than 
60 years.
1

## Page 373

3. The Land Tribunal rejected the Form No.7 filed by Respondent
no.1 by its order dated 09.06.1979. Aggrieved by the said order,
Respondent no.1 filed Writ Petition No. 3814 of 1980 before the
High Court of Karnataka, Bangalore (“High Court”). The learned
Single Judge of the High Court quashed the said order of the
Land Tribunal rejecting Form No.7 and remanded the case to the
Land Tribunal for a fresh enquiry. On remand, it was contended
by Respondent no.1, before the Land Tribunal, that his father
was the tenant under Sri Mahavalli Munithimappa and after coming
into force of the Karnataka Land Reforms Act, 1961, the subject
land  was  sold  by  Sri  Mahavalli  Munithimappa  in  favour  of
Munigeregappa. The Land Tribunal, vide order dated 10.07.2002,
again rejected the claim of Respondent no.1 in Form No.7 for
occupancy rights. This prompted Respondent no.1 to file Writ
Petition No. 32697 of 2002 before the High Court. The learned
Single Judge of the High Court rejected the Writ petition,
confirming the order of the Land Tribunal. Aggrieved, Respondent
no.1 preferred Writ Appeal No. 3724 of 2005 (LR), which was
dismissed for non-prosecution on 27.06.2006. 
4. Subsequently, the Appellants purchased the land in question
from the legal heirs of Munigeregappa, who was Respondent no.3
in the Writ Appeal, by a registered sale deed dated 07.08.2006,
which was registered on 13.09.2006. The Revenue Authorities
mutated the names of the Appellants and recorded their names in
the RTC for the year 2010–11. The Respondents subsequently got
the Writ Appeal restored and moved an Impleadment Application
2

## Page 374

before the High Court seeking the impleadment of the Appellants
herein, who had stepped into the shoes of the owners of the
land. 
5. The High Court  vide the impugned order allowed the Writ
Appeal filed by Respondent no.1 and set aside the judgment and
order passed by the learned Single Judge. Being aggrieved, the
Appellants approached this Court. Notice was issued by this
Court on 02.11.2012 and the parties were directed to maintain
status  quo  in respect of the land in question. Subsequently,
leave was granted on 09.01.2015, and the interim orders were
directed to continue till the disposal of the Civil Appeal.
6. During the pendency of this Civil Appeal, the parties have
arrived  at  a  settlement  and  they  have  jointly  moved  an
application (I.A. No. 208865 of 2026) under Order XXIII Rule 3
of the Civil Procedure Code, 1908 to place on record the terms
of compromise and to record the said compromise.
7. Today, when the matter was called out, the learned counsel
representing both sides confirmed, on instructions, that the
compromise have been entered into between the parties and the
full and final settlement have been arrived at. The parties
jointly agreed that the compromise may be taken on record and
the Civil Appeal may be disposed of in terms of the said
compromise,  which  is  marked  as  Annexure  A-1  to  the  joint
application along with joint affidavits (Annexure A-2) of all
the parties, who are signatories to the registered Confirmation
Deed and Full and Final Settlement Agreement. In accordance with
3

## Page 375

the same, it was confirmed that total consideration of Rs. 2.7
crores would be paid by the Appellants to the LRs of Respondent
no. 1, out of which, 50% of the payment had been made at the
time of execution of the settlement terms. During the course of
proceedings, the balance payment of 50% was handed over through
Demand Draft(s). 
8. Accordingly, the registered Confirmation Deed and Full and
Final  Settlement  Agreement  dated  21.05.2026,  signed  by  the
parties, along with the joint affidavit in confirmation of the
settlement, is taken on record and the Civil Appeal is disposed
of in terms of the same.
9. The Annexure A-1 and A-2 will form part of this order.  The
Parties shall abide by all terms and conditions as agreed.
10. The Civil Appeal is disposed of accordingly.

AJEET KUMAR @ AJIT KUMAR      APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
THE STATE OF BIHAR & ANR.     RESPONDENT(S)
ORDER
1. We have heard  Mrs. Anjana Prakash,  learned Senior
counsel for the appellant and Mr. Divyansh Mishra, learned
counsel for the respondent-State of Bihar.
2. Leave granted.
3. Appellant  takes  exception  to  the  order  dated
27.04.2026 passed by the High Court of Judicature at Patna
(briefly the ‘High Court’ hereinafter), rejecting the
regular bail application of the appellant.
4. Appellant  is  an  accused  in  Crime  No.43/2023
registered at Police Station- Buxar Town, District- Buxar,
Bihar under Sections 409, 406 and 420 of the Indian Penal
Code, 1860 (for short, ‘IPC’) read with Sections 120B/34
of the said Code.
5. Allegation against the appellant is that appellant
1

## Page 403

was an employee of Bihar State Seed Corporation Collection
Centre at Buxar. It is alleged that while serving so, he
had purchased 1291 quintals of wheat from the farmers
worth Rs.26,01,315/- but did not pay any money to the
farmers. Further allegation is that when the farmers asked
for their money, appellant had issued a cheque for an
amount of Rs.25,00,000/- in favour of the farmers, which
was dishonoured upon presentation.
6. Appellant was arrested on 21.10.2024 and since then,
he has been in custody.
7. This Court vide order dated 23.07.2026 had issued
notice, pursuant to which respondent-State of Bihar has
filed counter affidavit.
8. Learned Senior counsel for the appellant submits that
the allegation against the appellant is highly improbable.
Appellant being a lowly placed employee, would have no
competence to purchase such a huge quantity of wheat. The
case appears to be of false implication to cover up the
misdeeds of some higher ups. She further submits that the
core of the accusation against the appellant is that he
had issued a cheque to pay the farmers, cannot be believed
for the simple reason that there is no trace of the
cheque. Having regard to the period of detention undergone
by the appellant, she submits that appellant may be
enlarged on bail.
9. Learned counsel for the respondent-State of Bihar, on
the other hand, has referred to the averments made in the
2

## Page 404

counter affidavit and submits that appellant has a history
of committing similar offences. He submits that appellant
has 09 criminal antecedents but details of only 05 have
been  mentioned  in  paragraph  No.13  of  the  counter
affidavit.  Having  regard  to  the  seriousness  of  the
allegations against the appellant, he may not be enlarged
on bail, at this stage.
10. In  her  reply,  learned  Senior  counsel  for  the
appellant submits that in 05 of those cases mentioned by
the respondent-State of Bihar, appellant is on bail. That
apart, investigation is complete whereafter charge-sheet
has been submitted before the Court, though trial has not
yet  commenced.  Continuing  with  the  detention  of  the
appellant, in such circumstances, would not be justified.
11. Submissions made by learned counsel for the parties
have received the due consideration of the Court.
12. Having regard to the fact that investigation is
complete but trial has not yet commenced and also the fact
that appellant is in custody since 21.10.2024, we are of
the view that a case for grant of bail is made out.
13. Accordingly, t he  impugned  order  dated  27.04.2026
passed by the High Court is set aside. Consequently, we
direct that the appellant shall be produced before the
jurisdictional Judicial Magistrate within a maximum period
of 07 days from today, whereafter he shall be released on
bail on such terms and conditions as may be deemed
appropriate.
3

15. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO.12165 OF 2026
(Arising out of S.L.P.(Civil) No.29054 of 2026)
DELHI TRANSCO LIMITED  ... APPELLANT(S) 
                  VS.
SHYAM SUNDER B AMBWANI & ORS.            ... RESPONDENT(S)
                                                                   
          O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. Heard  Ms.  Lavanya  Kaushik,  learned  counsel
appearing  for  the  appellant  and  Mr.  Siddharth  Dave,
learned  senior  counsel  appearing  for  the  contesting
respondent Nos. 1 to 9.
3. The  present  appeal  calls  in  question  the
correctness of the order dated 30 th July, 2026 passed by
the High Court of Delhi at New Delhi in CM.APPL No.
33406/2026 filed in LA.APP No.16 of 2026.  By the said
order, the High Court, after noticing that the appellant
herein  has  deposited  100%  of  the  decretal  amount,
directed that 50% of the amount with accrued interest as
deposited, be released to the respondents on furnishing
an indemnity bond with an undertaking by way of an
affidavit stating that in the event the appellant herein
1

## Page 417

(appellant before the High Court) succeeds, the amount
would  be  returned  forthwith  to  them  with  reasonable
interest.  The High Court with regard to the remaining
50%  directed that  the remaining  50% along  with the
accrued interest shall be released on furnishing adequate
security to the satisfaction of the Executing Court.
4. Having heard learned counsel for the parties, we
are of the opinion that 50% of the deposited amount with
accrued  interest  be  released  to  the  respondents  on
furnishing adequate security to the satisfaction of the
Executing  Court. The  remaining 50%  ought not  to be
released, at this stage, and shall be kept in an interest
bearing fixed deposit in a Nationalized bank on auto-
renewal basis.
5. Hence, we vacate that portion of the impugned order
which directs release of 50% of the decretal amount with
accrued  interest based  on an  indemnity bond  and an
undertaking by way of an affidavit. The respondents shall
be entitled to the release of 50% of the deposited amount
with accrued interest and they shall furnish adequate
security to the satisfaction of the Executing Court.
6. We  also  direct  that  considering  that  the
acquisition is of 1963 and the land-owners have been
waiting for more than six decades, the High Court should
make an endeavour to hear the land acquisition appeals at
the earliest,  The High Court may endeavour to hear the
appeals within the next six months.
2

in the above terms.

CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.       OF 2026
(arising out of SLP(Crl.) No. 15533/2026)
DHARMENDRA KUMAR ..... APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
STATE OF BIHAR & ORS. ..... RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. The appellant, Dharmendra Kumar, approached the High Court of
Judicature at Patna by way of Criminal Miscellaneous No.
15460/2025 seeking cancellation of the anticipatory bail
granted to respondent Nos. 2 and 3 herein alleging that
sufficient grounds were made out for such cancellation.  
3. By the impugned order dated 29.07.2026, a learned Judge of
the High Court opined that he could not sit in appeal over
the  exercise  of  discretion  by  the  coordinate  Bench  in
granting anticipatory bail to respondent Nos. 2 and 3.  
4. The learned Judge seems to have lost sight of the fact that
the appellant had sought cancellation of the anticipatory
bail and had cited grounds therefor.  It was not a case of
the grant of bail itself being subjected to challenge, by way
of a petition for cancellation.
1

## Page 421

5. This  aspect  of  the  matter  required  to  be  examined
independently to ascertain whether any of the alleged grounds
cited  by  the  appellant  were  established  and  warranted
cancellation of the bail earlier granted. Such an exercise
did not entail the learned Judge sitting in appeal over the
grant of anticipatory bail by a coordinate Bench.  The order
passed  by  the  learned  Judge  is,  therefore,  utterly
misconceived and is liable to be set aside.
6. As all the parties are before this Court, there is no reason
as to why this appeal should be kept pending.  The appeal is,
accordingly,  allowed,  setting  aside  the  order  dated
29.07.2026 passed by the High Court.  
7. Criminal Miscellaneous No. 15460/2025 shall stand restored to
the file of the High Court for consideration afresh on merits
and in accordance with law.
Pending application(s), if any, stand disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO(S).      /2026
@ SLP (C) NO.22567/2026
M/S ANCL AND CO. (INDIA) PVT LTD. APPELLANT(S)
                                VERSUS
M/S JAGRAN SOCIAL WELFARE SOCIETY & ANR.            RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Heard
2. Leave granted.
3. The appellant and respondent entered into a contract on 14.11.2008 for
carrying out construction work, containing an arbitration clause whereunder the
President of the respondent(s) Society was agreed to be nominated as a sole
arbitrator. On purported completion of the project, the appellant is said to have
raised the bill and dispute between the parties having arisen on account of
alleged delay in completion of the project, resulted in arbitration proceedings
being initiated. In fact, no notice under Section 21 of the Arbitration and
Conciliation Act, 1996 (“the Act”) was issued.
4. Be that as it may, the sole arbitrator is said to have proceeded to
1

## Page 437

adjudicate the claim of the respondent(s) herein by placing the appellant ex
parte. Hence, an ex parte  arbitral award came to be passed on 16.08.2011 for
Rs.75,00,000/-. On various grounds appellant filed a petition under Section 34 of
the Act which came to be dismissed after eight years, i.e., on 17.03.2020. Being
aggrieved by the same, an appeal in Arbitration Appeal No.35/2020 under
Section 37 has been filed which is pending before the High Court. An application
for grant of stay of the award was also filed seeking absolute stay of the award
on the ground of procedural illegality. By the impugned order, the High Court
allowed the said application in part and directed the appellant herein to deposit
50% of the award amount as pre-condition for stay. Hence, this appeal.
5. This Court while issuing notice by order dated 09.07.2026 had stayed
further proceedings in Execution (Comm.) No.253/2022 which was pending
before the Court of District and Sessions Judge, South-East, Saket, New Delhi.
The said order of stay is in operation till date.
6. Though the learned counsels appearing for the parties would raise several
contentions, we refrain from scrutinizing the same for the simple reason that
any scrutiny or examination of the rival contentions is likely to prejudice their
rights in the appeal pending before the jurisdictional High Court. We are of the
view if request is made, the High Court to dispose of Arbitration Appeal
No.35/2020 expeditiously and preferably within six months from today it would
suffice. The stay of execution proceedings which came to be granted by this
Court if ordered to continue during the pendency of the appeal before the High
Court would meet the ends of justice. It is needless to state that the
jurisdictional High court would be at liberty to pass such other and further
orders as it deems fit while disposing of the appeal by putting the parties to
terms if they so desire. Accordingly, the appeal stands allowed in part. 
2

## Page 438

7. Pending application(s), if any, stands consigned to records. No orders as
to costs.

1. The applicants are allottees/legal heirs of the allottees, to
whom the State of Gujarat had allotted plots in Gandhi Nagar,
Gujarat. It appears that the allottees had initially joined the
government service. They retired a long time ago, and some of them
have now unfortunately passed away. The applicants seek permission
in terms of the order dated 02.11.2012 passed by this Court, to
sell the said plots allotted to them or their predecessors.
2. Keeping in view the hardships expressed by the applicants,
permission is granted to them to sell the allotted plots, subject

of these proceedings and a recital to this fact shall be duly
incorporated in the conveyance/sale deeds.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.           OF 2026
[ARISING OUT OF SLP (CRIMINAL) NO.8201 OF 2026]
PULENDRA SINGH & ANR.                     Appellant(s)
VERSUS
STATE OF UTTAR PRADESH                   Respondent(s)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. The appellants Pulendra Singh and Valister have
been convicted and sentenced in the following manner:
S.No. Section Sentence
1. Under Section 323 IPC R.I. for one year with fine
2. Under Section 504 IPC R.I. for two years with fine
3. Under Section 506 IPC R.I. for two years with fine
4. Under Section 324 IPC R.I. for two years and six 
months with fine
3. Admittedly, both the appellants have undergone
the entire sentence. However, as against the appellant
no.2-Valister, the injured Shripal has entered into a
compromise, which was filed before the High Court
under the caption "Joint Compromise Affidavit". 
4. The High Court, while affirming the judgment and
conviction  rendered  by  the  trial  Court,  has  not
considered the joint compromise affidavit, although
1

## Page 465

the High Court has converted the offence under Section
307 Indian Penal Code, 1860 ('IPC' for short) to one
under Section 324 Code of Criminal Procedure 1973
('CrPC' for short).
5. Thus, even if offence under Section 307 IPC was
not compoundable, once it is converted to an offence
under Section 324 CrPC, the same is compoundable under
Section 320 CrPC.
6. Shri  Meenesh  Kumar  Dubey,  learned  counsel
appearing for the appellants would submit that the
appellant no.2-Valister is a Home Guard. Therefore,
non-consideration of the compromise affidavit by the
High  Court  is  an  illegality  which  needs  to  be
corrected. 
7. He would submit that if the compromise is not
accepted and a consequential order is not passed, the
appellant no.2 shall lose his job.
8. The compromise affidavit has been filed by the
appellant no.2 which is placed in the record of the
appeal.
9. Having perused the joint compromise affidavit
filed  by  the  appellant  no.2-Valister  and  injured
Shripal before the High Court, we are inclined to
accept  the  compromise  affidavit  and  direct  that
2

## Page 466

appellant  no.2  Valister  be  acquitted  of  all  the
charges in view of the provisions contained in Section
320  (8)  CrPC  corresponding  to  359  (8)  Bharatiya
Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023.
10. Accordingly, the criminal appeal is allowed qua
respondent no.2-Valister.
11. If appellant no.2 has been terminated on account
of his conviction, he shall be reinstated due to the
consequential legal effect of Section 320 (8) CrPC.
The appellant is deemed to be acquitted of all the
charges.
12. The appeal qua respondent no.1 Pulendra Singh is
dismissed.
. . . . . . . . . . . . . ,J
[PRASHANT KUMAR MISHRA]   
. . . . . . . . . . . . . ,J

CRIMINAL APPEAL  NO.                   OF 2026

 RAMKUMAR @ RAMU                     APPELLANT(S)
                         VERSUS
 STATE REP. BY THE INSPECTOR 
 OF POLICE              RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. We have heard the learned counsel appearing for
the appellant and the learned counsel appearing
for the respondent. 
3. A limited notice was issued with respect to the
quantum of sentence alone. 
4. The appellant was charged and convicted by the
Trial Court for the offences punishable under
Sections 307 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 and
Section 4 of the Tamil Nadu Prohibition of
Harassment of Woman Act, 1988 and sentenced
accordingly to undergo rigorous imprisonment for
a period of seven years along with fine. The
judgment of conviction and the order on sentence
have been confirmed by the High Court, vide the
1 SLP(CRL.) No. 1557/2025

## Page 481

impugned  order.  Aggrieved  by  the  same,  the
appellant is before us. 
5. The learned counsel appearing for the appellant
submits that occurrence was of the year 2012,
and was pursuant to a love affair. The appellant
has been under incarceration for a period of
more than two years. 
6. The  learned  counsel  appearing  for  the
respondent-State submits that considering the
nature of injuries suffered by the victim, there
is  no  need  for  any  interference  with  the
impugned order.
7. Upon hearing the learned counsel appearing for
the parties, we do find mitigating circumstances
for the reduction of sentence. Admittedly, the
alleged occurrence took place in the year 2012,
when the victim spurned the offer made by the
appellant.  The  appellant  has  been  under
incarceration for a period of more than two
years.  His  conduct  while  undergoing
incarceration is also reasonably good.
8. Taking  note  of  the  aforesaid  mitigating
circumstances, we are inclined to modify the
sentence to the period already undergone by the
2 SLP(CRL.) No. 1557/2025

## Page 482

appellant. 
9. Accordingly, while confirming the conviction,
the sentence imposed stands modified to the
period already undergone by the appellant. The
appellant shall be released forthwith, unless
his custody is required in any other case.
10. The appeal stands allowed in part, accordingly. 
11. Pending  application(s),  if  any,  shall  stand
disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL ORIGINAL JURISDICTION
ARBITRATION PETITION NO.43 OF 2025
BEST ORGANIC INGREDIENTS PTY.
LTD. PETITIONER(S)
VERSUS
EXPOVAN RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. This petition under Section 11(5) of the Arbitration and
Conciliation Act, 1996 (Act) seeks the appointment of a sole
arbitrator to adjudicate disputes arising from a Memorandum of
Understanding dated 26.05.2024, executed between the Petitioner(s)
and the Respondent(s).
2. Briefly observed, the Petitioner, Best Organic Ingredients
Pty. Ltd., is an Australian entity engaged in the business of trade
and supply of various organic food products, including vanilla
beans.  Respondent  No.  1,  Expovan,  is  a  partnership  firm
incorporated in India. Respondent Nos. 2 and 3 are partners in the
Respondent No. 1-firm, while Respondent No. 4 is the firm’s Head of
Business Development. The Petitioner company, on various occasions,
sold vanilla beans to the Respondent No. 1-firm.
3. It is alleged that Respondent No. 1 began defaulting on
payments due to the Petitioner from July 2020. After various
communications and complaints, the parties arrived at a settlement
recorded in a Memorandum of Understanding dated 26.05.2024, under
which Respondent No. 1 acknowledged an outstanding amount of USD
1

## Page 501

500,000 and committed to clearing the same through staggered
payments by the third week of June 2024. Clause 7 of the Memorandum
provides that disputes not resolved through mutual discussion shall
be referred to arbitration, with the seat in India and the language
of arbitration being English.
4. It is further contended that Respondent No. 1 has again failed
to make its payments in terms of the Memorandum of Understanding.
It appears that the attempts to amicably settle the disputes
through mutual discussion between the parties also failed. In these
circumstances,  the  Petitioner  sought  to  initiate  arbitral
proceedings and issued an arbitration notice dated 20.12.2024. It
suggested  the  name  of  Mr.  Ashish  Batra,  Advocate,  as  the
arbitrator. However, the Respondent has not responded to the
notice. Hence, the Petitioner has filed the instant Petition,
seeking appointment of a sole arbitrator.
5. We have heard learned counsel for the parties and perused the
material placed on record.
6. Keeping in view the facts and circumstances recorded above and
the relevant provision under the Memorandum of Understanding dated
24.05.2024, we deem it just and proper to allow the instant
Arbitration Petition and appoint Justice R Suresh Kumar, former
Judge, Madras High Court as the Sole Arbitrator to resolve the
disputes between the parties. Keeping in view the facts and
circumstances of this case, the seat and venue of arbitration shall
be Chennai, India.
2

## Page 502

7. The  Arbitrator  shall  have  the  liberty  to  fix  his  own
remuneration/fees. Ordered accordingly.
8. Pending  interlocutory  applications,  if  any,  also  stand
disposed of.

2026 passed by the High Court of Punjab and Haryana at
Chandigarh in CRM-M No.12326 of 2026. By the said order,
the High Court has dismissed the bail application of the
petitioner in connection with FIR No.313 of 2018 dated
29th August, 2018 registered at Police Station Chandhut,
District Palwal, Haryana under Sections 302, 201, 34,
467, 468, 471 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 and Section
25 of Arms Act, 1959. 
3. We have considered the submissions of the learned
counsel for the parties. It is not disputed that the
petitioner, as an undertrial, has undergone 7 years and
11 months in custody. The trial is expected to take a
long time, since at least 15 more witnesses are yet to be
examined by the prosecution.
4. Considering the overall facts and circumstances,
we are  inclined to  enlarge the  petitioner on  bail,
pending trial.

CRIMINAL APPEAL NOS.                   OF 2026

MANMOHAN SINGH     APPELLANT
                        VERSUS
STATE OF JHARKHAND      RESPONDENT
O R D E R
1. Heard.
2. Leave granted.
3. Under the impugned order dated 15.12.2025, the High Court while
granting the bail had imposed the condition directing the appellant to furnish a
security bond equal to the alleged tax and penalty amount of approximately
Rs.30.21 Crores which the appellant claimed was impossible to comply and
onerous. The co-accused against whom similar condition was imposed had
approached this Court, namely, the son of the appellant herein in SLP (Crl.)
Nos.7344-7345/2026 which came to be disposed of by modifying the order as
under:
“6. In the aforesaid facts and circumstances of the case, we
are of the opinion that the condition imposed is onerous/vague and
cannot be given effect to. However, we direct that the petitioner
would furnish the security of the assets disclosed in the affidavit in
place of the condition of submitting a security bond equal to the
amount of tax and penalty.
7.Subject to the petitioner furnishing the security of the assets as
disclosed in the affidavit he shall be released on bail without
1

## Page 554

insisting for complying with the condition 42(C) of the impugned
bail order.”
4. Appellant contends he is on the same footing and the wife of the appellant
having already filed an affidavit disclosing entire assets of the family and
appellant being already on bail, we order that respondent shall not insist for
complying with condition No.45(c). Accordingly, the appeal stands allowed. It is
also made clear that the assets declared by the mother shall constitute security
for the alleged amount due. 
5. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

“a) Pass an ex-parte ad-interim order directing the Respondent Nos. 1 to

applicants’
b) Direct the Respondents Nos.1 to 4 to allow the applicants (original
petitioners No.1 to 8) to continue to serve like other similarly situated
persons;
C) In the alternative direct Respondent Nos. 1 to 4 to treat the applicants
as continuing in service till the age of 60 years and give all service
benefits, emoluments and allowances, subject to the outcome of the
present SLP.
d) Pass such other order/orders as may be deemed fit and proper in the
facts and circumstances of the case.”
2. This Court by order dated 27.07.2026 had stayed the operation of the
impugned judgment and order until further orders. It is the grievance of the
applicants that eight of them have been relieved prior to the order passed by
this Court and subsequent to the filing of the present Special Leave Petition. In
view of the subsequent event having taken place, question of putting the clock
back does not arise at this stage. Hence, question of considering their prayer for
being reinstated into service at this stage would not be appropriate. The prayer
sought for in the application stands rejected. However, we make it clear that in
the event of these applicants succeeding in the present matter, they would be
entitled for all the consequential reliefs.

Additional Advocate General (AAG) appearing for the

2. The petitioner calls in question the correctness of
the order dated 09-03-2026 in MCRC No. 4766/2026 passed
by the High Court of Madhya Pradesh at Gwalior. By the
said order, the petitioner has been denied the benefit
of  bail  in  connection  with  FIR/Crime  No.15/2022
(Session  Case  No.19/2025)  registered  with  Kolaras
Police Station, District Shivpuri, Madhya Pradesh, for
the offences punishable under Sections 420, 409, 467,
468, 471 & 120B of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 and
undler Sections 13(1)(a) & 13(2) of the Prevention of
Corruption Act, 1988.
3. Learned Senior Counsel for the petitioner contends
that the petitioner has already undergone about one
year & six months in custody in the aforesaid FIR.
Learned Senior Counsel fairly points out that the
petitioner has already one conviction in the other
case(FIR  No.386/2021)  and  sentenced  to  five  years
imprisonment in the said case where the petitioner had
already undergone about three years & six months, when
his sentence was suspended. Learned Senior Counsel
draws attention of the Court to the bail granted to the
co-accused- Rakesh Kumar Kulshrestha. 
4. Learned  AAG  appearing  for  the  State,  however,
vehemently opposes the bail prayer of the petitioner
and submits that apart from the prior conviction of the

## Page 564

3
petitioner, the amount involved in the case, is also of
a high order.
5. Considering the overall facts and circumstances of
the case; the period undergone by the petitioner; the
likelihood of time to be taken by the Trial Court and
keeping the fact that the co-accused has also been
enlarged on bail, we are inclined to enlarge the
petitioner on bail.
6. Accordingly,  we  direct  that  the  petitioner  be
enlarged on bail su bject to the satisfaction of the
concerned Trial Court in connection with the aforesaid
FIR for the offences mentioned hereinabove.
7. The Special Leave Petition is disposed of in the
above terms.
8. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand
disposed of.

The petitioner is an accused in a proceeding under
Section  138  of  the  Negotiable  Instruments  Act,  1881,
initiated by the respondent herein.
2. The 4 th Additional Chief Judicial Magistrate’s Court at
Anand,  Gujarat,  before  which  the  proceedings  were
initiated,  dismissed  the  complaint  and  acquitted  the
accused. On appeal, the Principal District and Sessions
1

## Page 566

Judge, Anand, reversed the order of the Trial Court and
convicted the petitioner and imposed a sentence of one year
of imprisonment along with a fine of double of the cheque
amount.
3. In the revision filed by the petitioner before the High
Court of Gujarat, by the impugned order, the accused was
directed to surrender before the Trial Court and the matter
was directed to be listed on 22.09.2026 for reporting the
due surrender. 
4. When the matter came up before this Court, we granted an
interim order subject to the petitioner depositing an
amount of 20% of the cheque amount with the Registry of the
High Court of Gujarat.
5. Today, when the matter was taken up, learned counsel for
the  petitioner  informed  us  that  the  amount  has  been
deposited as directed. The respondent also appeared and
contended that, in fact, for a stay of the sentence, the
statutory prescription is remittance of 20% of the total
fine amount and not the cheque amount.
6. This is a case of divergent finding where the Trial
Court dismissed the complaint and the First Appellate Court
reversed it. 
7. Only to secure ends of justice, especially, on the
peculiar facts and circumstances of this case, we direct
the revision itself to be heard without requiring the
surrender  of  the  petitioner/accused  to  undergo  the
sentence. Disbursement of the amounts deposited by the
2

orders to be passed.

directions.

Section 7 of the Chhattisgarh Gambling (Prohibition) Act,
2022. 
2. Charge-sheet No.102 of 2026 was filed on 10.06.2026,
including Section 112(2) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita,
2023. The petitioner was named in the charge-sheet as
Accused No.21/Babu alias Gulshan Khemani, arrested on
17.04.2026.
3. The petitioner along with others are accused of being
involved in an organized online gambling group, which
runs online cricket betting through an app called “3
Stumps”, based on disclosure statements of co-accused. 
4. Learned counsel for the Petitioner submitted that four
of the co-accused have been granted bail by this court.

petitioner husband seeks transfer of Matrimonial Suit No. 1967 of

the Court of Principal Judge, Family Court, Aligarh, Uttar Pradesh
to the Court of Principal Judge, Family Court, South West District,
Dwarka, New Delhi.
2. Heard the learned counsel appearing for the parties and
perused the materials available on record, including the counter
affidavit filed by the respondent - wife.

husband warranting transfer of the case, as prayed for by him, the
Transfer  Petition  deserves  to  be  allowed.  It  is  ordered
accordingly.
4. Consequently, Matrimonial Suit No. 1967 of 2024 titled "Neha
Roma Adhikari vs. Pankaj Marwah" pending before the Court of
Principal Judge, Family Court, Aligarh, Uttar Pradesh is ordered to
be transferred to the Court of Principal Judge, Family Court, South
West District, Dwarka, New Delhi.

A W A R D
1. The controversy in this case pertains to payment of back
wages and other service benefits for the period during which the
appellant remained out of service as a result of his conviction
under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988. That judgment was
passed on 27.01.2014 and consequent thereupon, the appellant was
discharged from service w.e.f. 21.10.2014. He, however, earned
acquittal from the High Court vide judgment dated 20.04.2017 and
the respondent-bank, without any inordinate delay, reinstated him
vide order dated 12.09.2017. However, wages for the period from
21.10.2014 to 11.09.2017 have not been paid to the appellant.  
2. The appellant is present in person.

## Page 629

2
3. During settlement, the appellant graciously agreed to
accept a lump sum amount of Rs.15,00,000/- (fifteen lakhs). We have
also persuaded the respondent-bank to pay the aforesaid amount of
Rs.15,00,000/- (fifteen lakhs) along with simple interest at the
rate of 6% per annum w.e.f. 01.01.2019 till the date of payment.
The payment shall be made by the respondent-bank to the appellant
within three weeks.
4. It goes without saying that other consequential service
benefits shall also be granted to the appellant.  
5. The appeal stands disposed of in terms of the Award.

2. The matter has been heard on a number of occasions and the

4. In view of what has transpired during the proceedings, the
final offer made by the petitioner-husband is that he would clear
all past arrears towards maintenance/compensation, quantified at
Rs. 28,40,000/- (Rupees Twenty Eight Lakhs and Forty Thousand). In
addition thereto, the petitioner-husband has offered to provide the
respondent-wife  with  a  three-bedroom  apartment  and  a  sum  of
Rs. 20,00,000/- (Rupees Twenty Lakhs) in cash in lieu of the
monthly maintenance of Rs. 25,000/- (Rupees Twenty Five Thousand).
5. In the alternative, having regard to the stand taken by the
respondent-wife, it is submitted that in lieu of the payment of
Rs. 20,00,000/- (Rupees Twenty Lakhs), the petitioner-husband would
continue to pay maintenance to the respondent-wife at the rate of
Rs. 25,000/- (Rupees Twenty Five Thousand) per month. It has
further been stated by the petitioner-husband, who is also present
in Court, that he would bear the actual expenses of his son’s
education and that the son would continue to retain all his rights
in future arising from his status as the biological son of the
petitioner-husband.
6. Though the respondent-wife, when heard by the Court, has taken
the stand that she is not amenable to the grant of divorce, learned
counsel appearing for the respondent-wife submits that one further
opportunity may be granted to the respondent-wife to explore the

possibility of arriving at a settlement.

on record in detail.

submitted that in the interregnum, the impugned order
has been given effect to inasmuch as the possession of
the  scheduled  shop  has  been  taken  over  by  the
receiver.
6. If that is so, we direct the receiver to handover the
possession of the scheduled shop to the petitioner
herein and file a report in that regard to this Court
within a period of two weeks from today.
7. At this stage, learned senior counsel appearing for
respondent No.1/caveator submitted that the interim
order may be made absolute and the Special Leave
Petition could be disposed of with a direction to the
Trial Court to conclude the trial expeditiously.
8. In response, petitioner’s counsel submitted that she
has no objection for such an order being passed.
9. In the circumstances, we dispose of this Special Leave
Petition by making the aforesaid interim order final.
10. The  Special  Leave  Petition  stands  disposed  of.
However, since the suit is of the year 1976, we direct
the Trial Court to conclude the same as expeditiously

year from today.

Heard learned counsel for the parties.
2. In view of the fact that as per paragraph no.17 of the
impugned order dated 01.08.2025, the High Court has directed that
the respondent’s service rendered as a temporary employee from
1976, be added to the petitioner’s service post-absorption in the
establishment so that he fulfills minimum requisite ten years
qualifying  service  for  grant  of  pensionary  benefits  meaning
thereby, that the short-fall of about three and a half years when

## Page 773

2
the respondent worked in unabsorbed capacity, will only be counted
and added to the period he worked in regular capacity so as to make
him eligible for grant of pensionary benefits, we do not find any
error in the same warranting interference by this Court.
3. We further note that similar matter being SLP(C) No.16216 of
2026 has been dismissed by this Court vide order dated 04.05.2026.
4. Accordingly, the present petition also stands dismissed.
5. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

owner/revenue khata holder intimating the deposit along with proof of same.

Collector-cum-District Magistrate, Land Acquisition, Greater Noida, Gautam
Buddha Nagar, Uttar Pradesh shall be personally be present before the Court.

1. The submission of the learned counsel for the
petitioner is that the High Court fell in error in
upholding the order of the trial court in respect of
award of interest at the rate of 24 per cent per
annum by placing reliance on invoices (Exhibit D-5
to  Exhibit  D-13)  which  were  not  between  the
plaintiff  and  the  defendant  but  between  the
defendant and a third party. Those invoices could

interest payable. Moreover, the interest at the rate
of 24 per cent per annum is unduly harsh and is not
sustainable under any circumstances.

condoned.
3. Issue notice, limited to the rate at which the
interest has been awarded, returnable in four weeks.

379 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (for short, ‘IPC’) and under
Sections 411 & 34 of IPC added later on.
3. When the matter came up for hearing on 29.05.2026, while
issuing notice, this Court had granted interim protection to
the petitioner.
4. Having perused the records; keeping the overall facts and
circumstances of the case, and the fact that the petitioner has
participated in the investigation, we confirm the order dated
29.05.2026 granting interim protection to the petitioner on the
same terms.

is disposed of.

1. Delay condoned.
2. Heard  Mr.Kanu  Agarwal,  learned  counsel  for  the
petitioner.  Learned  counsel  for  the  petitioner  drawing
attention to page 207 (pdf 269) a note of the Sub-Divisional
officer  dated  07.03.2015  submits  that  admittedly  though
Notification  under  Section  4  and  Section  6  of  the  Land
Acquisition Act 1894 (for short, ‘LAC, 1894’) were issued, no

## Page 981

2
award was passed in accordance with the provision of LAC,
1894. Learned counsel submits that in view of that, the
proceedings are deemed to have automatically lapsed, after the
expiry of the one year from the passing of the declaration
under Section 6 in accordance with the amendment of LAC, 1894.
Learned counsel contends that in view of this, the question of
approaching  the concerned  Reference Court  for enhancement
cannot arise. Learned counsel submits that the net result is
without a valid process, the petitioner has been deprived of
her valuable land. According to learned counsel the land which
has been taken over for road and school construction, is to an
extent of 0.634 hectares.
3. Issue notice, returnable on 30th October, 2026.
4. State to deal with the above contentions in the counter
affidavit in detail.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The present petition has been filed against order
dated 22.06.2026 in CRL.MP. No.10167 of 2026 passed by the
High Court of Madras at Chennai.
2. Learned counsel for the petitioner has stated before

## Page 1057

2
this Court that the High Court while granting bail to the
petitioner, imposed a condition to deposit a sum of Rs.11
lakhs  which  is  unreasonable  and  difficult  for  the
petitioner to comply with.
3. Learned counsel for the respondent-State has stated
before this Court that initially while granting bail to the
petitioner vide order dated 30 th April, 2026, six weeks’
time was granted to deposit a sum of Rs.11 lakhs; however,
the same was not done by the petitioner resulting in
cancellation of bail.
4. Learned  counsel  for  the  petitioner  has  further
stated before this Court that the petitioner is in jail.
5. After hearing the learned counsel for the parties,
this Court is of the opinion that the matter deserves to be
heard on merits by the High Court. The impugned order is
hereby set aside and the High Court shall be free to pass
appropriate orders after hearing both the parties.
6. Keeping in view the aforesaid, the High Court is
requested to decide the matter at an early date.
7. With  the  above  observations,  the  Special  Leave
Petition stands disposed of.
8. Pending applications(s), if any, shall also stand
disposed of.

2. Mr. Amit Rawal, states that the respondent,
has little or for that matter, no defence on the
disobedience complained against the respondent. As an
Officer  of  the  Court  and  to  avoid  further
precipitation, he requests fifteen (15) days time
from today to vacate and deliver vacant possession of
the property to the petitioner herein.
3. Having due regard to the age of the respondent
and the seriousness with which the statement is made
by Mr. Amit Rawal, fifteen (15) days time, as prayed,
has been granted.
4. We make it clear that if at all the present
statement is not complied with, the Court while
continuing to examine the disobedience complained
against  the  respondent  and  will  direct  the
Superintendent  of  Police  to  take  possession  of
property from the respondent and hand it over to the
petitioner. Inasmuch as the breach of undertakings
given to the Courts, if are allowed to happen on a
regular basis, the same would amount to interfering
with the administration of justice.
5. List on 18.09.2026.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Delay condoned.
2. We have heard Mr. K.M. Nataraj, learned Additional Solicitor
General of India on behalf of the petitioner(s) and Mr. Shyam
Divan, learned Senior Counsel on behalf of the first respondent,
who is on Caveat.
3. In light of the categorical findings returned by the High
Court in Paragraph 62 of the Impugned Judgment, which are duly
supported by the averments made in the pleadings and the documents
on record, we are satisfied that the impugned judgment calls for no
interference.  However, we deem it appropriate to make it clear
that the claim of the decree-holder will firstly be satisfied
through the assets of the judgment debtor, namely UCM Coal Company
Limited, and it is only if the claim remains unsatisfied that the
execution proceedings against the petitioner(s) shall proceed.
4. With this clarification and modification, the Special Leave
Petition stands disposed of with pending application(s), if any.

order is to give an opportunity to the first respondent

1. The instant petition has been filed purportedly in public
interest seeking Court-monitored institutional reforms to address
the alleged negligible listing and disposal of appeals before the
Goods and Services Tax Appellate Tribunal (GSTAT).

petitioner in a representation addressed to the President, GSTAT.

any opinion, and with liberty to the petitioner to pursue the
representation dated 22.07.2026 addressed to the President, GSTAT.

into the grievance and find out the appropriate solution.
